speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask him whether the government has any intention of bringing in legislation at this session to implement any of the recommendations of the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects; and second, and in particular, whether it is the intention of the government to bring in any measures to encourage Canadian companies in business to compete successfully with foreign companies, such as by special tax concessions and the like, as recommended by the commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, the report of the commission was published only yesterday and will be given careful consideration. The hon. gentleman's question about competition by Canadian companies is in very

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT- WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Prime Minister. Could he tell the house if the government has made any undertaking with regard to the proposed waiver of $22 million in interest charges due by the United Kingdom?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT- WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the hon. member will see no objection to my answering his question in English since I will have to refer to statutes, and these references are in English. I have had no time to check


the French text and I should not like to make a free translation whose terms would probably not be those which the official translators have used in the French version of the statutes.
(Text):
The Canadian-United Kingdom loan agreement of 1946, which appears as a schedule to the United Kingdom Financial Agreement Act (1946, Chap. 12), provides that the United Kingdom is entitled to a waiver of interest in any year in which certain conditions exist. In brief, the Canadian loan agreement entitles the United Kingdom to a waiver when the following conditions are met:
(a)	That the United Kingdom finds it necessary, having regard to its gold and foreign exchange reserves;
(b)	That the international monetary fund certifies to certain specified conditions regarding United Kingdom balance of payments statistics; and
(c)	That any other country which has made a loan with similar conditions is also waiving the interest payment.
That is a commitment that was made in the contract that was approved by parliament in 1946. Early in December of last year the United Kingdom formally requested a waiver of the interest which would be due on the 31st of December, 1956. Because of another rather complicated clause in the United States-United Kingdom agreement relating to the status of certain sterling balances, a clause which is not in the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, the United States government found it lacked authority to grant the waiver, but it announced that it would renegotiate the waiver clause and submit a new clause to congress. That, of course, prevents one of the conditions under which the waiver would be contractually obligatory upon Canada from being realized.
The Canadian government is considering what action it would be appropriate for this government to take and as soon as this consideration has been completed the conclusion arrived at by the government will be put before parliament and there will be an opportunity to discuss it here in parliament.
In the meantime the United Kingdom has paid the instalment of principal amounting to $15J million which was due on December 31 and has, I understand, set aside in an account in the Bank of Canada the amount of interest, this to be held by the Bank of Canada until a decision has been reached whether or not there will be a waiver of interest granted by all those who have similar loans.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was congratulating the government for preserving the unity of the commonwealth at a time of particularly serious emergency and saving the world from a third world conflict. Canada has declared its opposition to wars of aggression and we must recognize that, in this regard, its position was sound, no economic interests to my mind being worth a single drop of blood. If some people are not yet convinced that problems should be solved by peaceful means, they must not count on our aid. If the unfortunate experiences of 1914 and 1939 have not been such as to cause them to reflect upon these matters, the world is indeed in desperate straits.
As President Eisenhower said yesterday to the United States Congress: "An aggressive war is a crime against humanity". That is also the opinion of Canada; we do not want to be parties to any crime.
It is precisely because Canada is opposed to crimes against humanity that at the General Assembly of the United Nations our
The Address-Mr. Caron representatives have condemned in unequivocal terms the repression by the Soviet Union of Hungarian patriots.
I had the great pleasure of entertaining in my own home, on Christmas day, a group of Hungarian refugees, one of whom spoke French and another English. These people told me things that we would have not thought possible in this twentieth century. A father, his wife and two children had to crawl several miles through mud to take cover from Russian Are. Russians were firing at them to prevent them from gaining their freedom. These people told me that story themselves and it was corroborated by another member of the group.
In Budapest, a woman and child were killed by soldiers for failing to stop when ordered to do so. All these refugees can thus recount instances of truly revolting brutality.
I am convinced that when this crisis of Russian imperialistic madness is over, those barbarians themselves will blush at their own deeds. I am happy to congratulate the government, and particularly the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill), for the promptness with which Canada opened its frontiers to those unfortunate victims of their love of freedom.
I also congratulate the government for wishing to endow Canada with a council for the arts, humanities and social sciences. If our country has reached political and economic maturity, it must now turn to things of the mind. To prevent Canadians from becoming merely poor imitators, we must endeavour to create a truly Canadian art, one which will not be a pathetic copy of imported art.
A question that has been and will continue to be widely discussed, both verbally and in print, is the matter of proposed government assistance to universities. It is high time for action in that field and the Prime Minister has had the courage to propose a formula designed to save those temples of knowledge from bankruptcy; but the Quebec dictator is opposed to it, unconcerned about what our nation will become without those institutions of high learning.
In a country expanding as rapidly as Canada is doing, there is a growing need of specialists in all fields, which only our universities can train.
Indeed, we already hear the laments of those who are responsible for this stagnation! They accuse us of being centralizers. They claim that, through these donations, the federal government infringes upon a field that is exclusively provincial, that of education.
But how and where can the millions of dollars given unconditionally to universities

The Address-Mr. Caron be considered as an intrusion in the field education?
With such reasoning, millionaires should no longer be permitted to bequeath part of their fortune to such institutions. Wealthy corporations should no longer be allowed to grant scholarships for special studies. That would be ridiculous. I would be prepared to agree with them if, in exchange for such grants, the government required changes of curriculum in this or that faculty but, as I said, an unconditional donation does not constitute interference.
In all parts of Canada, rectors of universities have gladly and gratefully accepted this offer from the federal government, except in Quebec, where fear of the master causes them to hesitate between a realization of the great need, and threats which are not even veiled.
It is high time that the leaders of our Quebec universities make up their mind to face up squarely to the dictator and tell him: "Take care, for in the end we will come out the winners; remember that spirit has always prevailed over brute force." Then you will see the type of turn about of which this tumbler is capable.
When I hear people find fault with this proposal of the federal government under the pretence of safeguarding our language and our faith, I am inclined to think that this is sheer demagogy.
If actually we had been meant to disappear as a racial entity, it is immediately after the conquest of 1760 that it would have happened, because at that time, the noble and the rich went back to France, leaving behind 60 thousand poor people, most of them illiterate, to fight it out by themselves, or just about, with the conquerors who, however, have respected treaties.
Now that this miracle of the survival of a handful of men has been brought about by Providence, it would be impossible to crush the six million French-speaking Canadians scattered all over Canada, most of whom live in the province of Quebec.
We have acquired such a strength that we now hold the balance of power in Ottawa, a fact that the Liberal party has understood much earlier than did the other parties which are still stagnating on the opposition side.
Moreover, so long have we been ruled by fear, that French Canadians still hesitate to play their full part in our great Canada.
Yes, our country is now an international power, an evolution which the Fathers of the Confederation could not foresee. That is why we must look and act as full-grown men in a great country which will soon have, I hope, a truly distinctive flag bearing no sign whatever of interdependence.

It is
not often, Mr. Speaker, that in the throne speech debate I concentrate exclusively on local matters. This year, as I look through the speech from the throne, unfortunately it does not provide too much opportunity to dwell on domestic problems because a large part of it is concerned with external policy. It could be argued, of course, that in view of the continuing international crisis this emphasis is important. We are still under the shadow of the crisis in Suez, and if those problems are not settled adequately there is very little use giving attention to domestic issues.
The speech from the throne is sometimes referred to as a state of the nation speech, and we should be able to cover the issues that are most pertinent in Canada at the present time, particularly those which concern our local constituencies. As far as the problems on the higher level of external and foreign policy are concerned, we hope there will be other occasions in this house during this session when we will be able to come to closer grips with these matters.
I notice that in their presentations both the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) concerned themselves with the matters that were closest to their constituencies. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, in his genial Irish way, very effectively presented the problems of his area, although I think perhaps he did not have much to say about those problems. He had definitely kissed the blarney stone in the traditional Irish sense, and he presented a picture that all was for the best in the best of possible worlds in Edmonton-Strath-cona. Then, too, the hon. member for Gloucester in his presentation ended on an optimistic note. He thought it was time that the maritimers forgot to be pessimistic and moved forward to emphasize the positive or the optimistic side of the picture. I am glad to know that he agrees that under the new regimes in the maritimes things are going to be much better in that part of the country.

speechtext:
I am going to crave the indulgence of the house to refer to some matters that are of immediate concern in the Brandon-Souris constituency. It is true the

speech from the throne talks in general terms about the continuing prosperity in Canada. However, I sometimes feel that on the Ottawa level we cannot see the woods for the trees, and while we can speak in grandiose terms about the general prevailing prosperity, sections of the economy have not participated in an equitable way in the general economic upsurge in Canada during the postwar years. However, I do not want to begin on that note, either.
One of the reasons why I am sticking to local matters in this address is that this year, in my particular corner of the country, we are entering upon anniversary observances which have some importance. These anniversary observances commenced some three years ago in southwestern Manitoba, an area that was settled in the early 1880's. In the past three years several of our communities have been observing 75th anniversaries. Two years ago the town of Deloraine had an observance of that kind. Last year it was the towns of Boissevain and Souris, and this year the towns of Killarney and Virden and the city of Brandon will be observing 75th anniversaries. It is an occasion when we are marking the achievements of the past and looking forward to the prospects of the future. The celebrating of 75 years of actual settlement and incorporation in that part of the world underlines the fact that we are a very young community in western Canada. There is to be another 75th anniversary this year. Very shortly, I believe, our Prime Minister will be celebrating his 75th birthday, his 75th anniversary. This also points out that actually within the lifetime of one man, who has assumed a very prominent role in this country, western Canada has progressed to the present relatively high state of organization and progress.
We are still a very young nation and while we sometimes feel we have not made very much progress in some parts of Canada this is perhaps due to our youthfulness and our anxiety to get on with the job, to seize the tremendous opportunities that are available to all Canadians today and also, of course, to seize the responsibilities arising from those opportunities.
My constituency which is presently called the constituency of Brandon-Souris existed as the constituency of Brandon until the redistribution in 1953. It is typical, I feel, of the type of social organization that has emerged in the west since settlement began in 1880. It has produced some of the most prominent men who have held a position of representation in this house.
From the year 1896 until about 1912, I believe, the late Sir Clifford Sifton was the
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale member for Brandon. It was under Sir Clifford's leadership that the tremendous upsurge in immigration took place in the early 1900's which assured that western Canada would assume a growing position of prominence in our Canadian economy. He established a pattern for immigration during those years that might well be followed by the present administration because in a comparatively short time some three million new citizens were brought into western Canada under his leadership.
Another important era in public life in this country was marked by another former member for Brandon, the late Hon. Robert Forke who for a few years was the leader of the Progressive party in this chamber. I think all hon. members will agree that very significant developments in public life on the national level emerged out of that period of politics in the twenties when the Progressive party played a prominent role.
I do not think I will be regarded as prejudiced if I say the Progressive movement, the farmers' movement in this country and particularly in western Canada, brought a fresh breath of air into public affairs which has had an influence right up to the present time. Certainly the Liberal party under the leadership of Mr. Mackenzie King, after he had absorbed the Progressive movement or certain aspects of it, was a very different Liberal party from the Liberal party that existed under the earlier regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. There was a new emphasis in Canadian public life. Not all of the things that emerged out of that movement were beneficial, of course. Sometimes we westerners are known as the wild and wooly westerners; sometimes perhaps we are regarded as being somewhat irresponsible or at least certain influences in western Canada are considered in that light. Nevertheless there were some beneficial influences that emerged out of the Progressive movement.
On opening day it was my privilege to attend the ceremonies held in connection with the unveiling of the monument to Sir Robert Borden. I found those ceremonies very impressive indeed and I was interested to hear the tributes that were paid to that outstanding Canadian leader and particularly the emphasis that was placed on the role he had played in establishing Canada's position as an autonomous nation amongst the British commonwealth of nations. It occurred to me at that time that had it not been for the fresh breezes that blew out of the west in the wake of the Progressive movement that introduced new ideas and emphases into Canadian public life it would not have been possible for Sir Robert Borden to have achieved the new status for

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale Canada. Certainly the wave of immigration under the leadership of Sir Clifford Sifton brought in new ideas and a new emphasis on national spirit that made it possible for Prime Minister Borden to declare a position of independence for Canada at the treaty of Versailles conferences without creating too much unfavourable reaction back home in Canada.
The fact exists as well that we had established our reputation as a responsible national power during the trial of world war I, but I still claim for western Canada that some of these new concepts, this fresh impetus and the new emphases made it possible for Canada to proceed one step further along the road toward becoming a nation among the nations of the world.
More recently we have had outstanding representatives from the constituency of Brandon in the persons of Colonel D. W. Beaubier, who represented that area during the difficult early thirties, the late Mr. J. E. Matthews, who at the time of his death was the dean of this house by point of age, and then of course, just prior to the amalgamation of the constituencies of Brandon and Souris, the latter constituency was represented by Mr. J. A. Ross who, like so many of those who have devoted the major part of their lives to public service, is unfortunately at the present time not enjoying good health. In the past two years he has unfortunately been suffering from ill health, a reaction to the strenuous exertion he put forward in this house for a period of 13 years on behalf of the people of the constituency I now have the honour to represent.
We have rather an illustrious history emerging from this part of southwestern Manitoba. It was the opening of western Canada which made it possible for the flow of golden grain which in many respects changed our whole national economic picture. In the early days Brandon became known as the wheat city of the west because it was the first point at which large shipments of wheat were received. John A. Macdonald's dream of national unity was only made possible when he conceived the whole plan of confederation on the opening up of western Canada and the beginning of our grain economy.
In those days the city of Brandon founded an agricultural exhibition. Perhaps they were a little ambitious when they called it the dominion agricultural exhibition. No doubt they hoped to occupy the place now occupied by the royal agricultural winter fair in the city of Toronto. Such was the spirit of those early pioneers who moved into that area. Somewhat later they had to be satisfied with calling their exhibition the provincial winter fair and the provincial ex-


hibition, but it is still one of the largest of its kind in the country and has made outstanding contributions to agricultural life.
That was the picture down through the years until fairly recently, perhaps we can say up to the commencement of world war II in 1939. More recently Brandon has become the home of the western Canada trade fair. I think that name nicely and aptly suggests the new pattern which is emerging in the western economy where you have the western Canada trade fair intimately associated with the provincial exhibition of Manitoba and the provincial winter fair.
There is a new order, if I may call it that, or a new era emerging in the prairie economy which has become clear to all hon. members from that part of the country. This is the picture which was presented by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona in his excellent remarks the other day. However, unfortunately the speech from the throne gives little indication that the present government is aware of what is taking place in western Canada. It gives little indication that the government is aware of the dynamic changes which are taking place.
I have had the preliminary report of the Gordon commission in my hands only overnight and have had an opportunity merely to scan it, but after scanning some of the main points in this interesting report I would say that here are a group of economists who have given serious thought to what is taking place in the Canadian economy at the present time, who have an appreciation of the changes that are taking place.
Looking at some of the sections of the report I find that their subject matters have been the topics of discussion in this house during recent months. I find reference to wheat, to the development of energy resources, the taxation of the oil and gas industries, secondary manufacturing industries, our commercial policy and foreign capital investment in Canada. After noting those I almost come to the conclusion that the commissioners responsible for the report had been looking over the shoulder of the Hon. George A. Drew or had been reading Hansard diligently to see the excellent analyses he had made of the situation during the past few years when it was my privilege to serve under his leadership in this house. I can almost say that he must have written part of this report.
Certainly it is a stimulating experience to find that those who have been charged with the responsibility for analysing our economy as it is and our future economic prospects have shown such a progressive and enlightened grasp of the situation. In many respects it is the viewpoint that we have held

in western Canada during recent years. It is a direct challenge to the government to do something about these things, to keep step with the dynamics of the economic and social changes which have been occurring in Canada, particularly since the end of world war II. It is a challenge to the government to do something about it or to step aside and let someone else meet the situation as it needs to be met at the present time.
There were some references in the speech from the throne to certain problems on the agricultural front. The agricultural picture has been far from bright in the past few years. Reference is made to a survey to be conducted in all parts of Canada of land use, and the suggestion is that the government is going to give consideration at long last to the possibility of establishing a legislative program for comprehensive conservation measures.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has been on the statute books ever since the days of the drought in the early thirties. As has been mentioned in this house, it is a tribute to the appreciation of the problem by the prime minister of that day, Mr. R. B. Bennett. Unfortunately it applies only to western Canada. Certainly a measure of this kind would be in the best interests of the Canadian economy as a whole, not only from the agricultural standpoint but also from the standpoint of the total picture.
Considering the rapidity with which our economy is developing at the moment, we must give serious attention to this problem of conservation on a national basis. During recent years certain private members have placed resolutions on the order paper covering this matter and we have had worth while discussions, but to amend the P.F.R.A. in an attempt to cope with this problem is to deal only with a small aspect of the total difficulties which face agriculture at the moment.
We are moving toward an industrial economy. It has become almost platitudinous to say that you cannot have a healthy economy or a healthy society unless you have a strong, solvent and progressive underlying agricultural industry. Unfortunately we do not have that at the present time. The industrial revolution which has hit western Canada has made serious inroads into our agricultural activity. The government has done nothing to deal with the changes which are taking place. These matters have been mentioned many times in the house. We have talked about the price squeeze under which the farmer is suffering. We have talked about the problems created by surplus production. However, perhaps the major difficulty is the general exodus of people from the farm.
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
These are only three of the subjects which require immediate action on the part of the present administration having regard to the nature of the economy in which we are operating at the present time and to the "price squeeze" in which the farmer finds himself. It is an inflationary economy-an economy key-noted by industrial development in which both capital and labour find themselves on a price escalator. It seems that no sooner do prices rise under the impact of creeping inflation than labour asks for an increase in wages. It is a fine, thrilling ride for those who largely derive their incomes from these two orders of activity, that is to say, capital and labour, but for those who are not on the "escalator" it presents a very difficult situation indeed. Those who do not benefit include, unfortunately, our farmers and those of our citizens in receipt of fixed incomes.
We have had many dramatic pleas in this house that some action should be taken which would at least place these people in receipt of fixed incomes on the first step of the stairway to better conditions even if they cannot ride the escalator which exerts such a heady influence on those who are riding it at the present time. We have heard appeals for war pensioners, appeals for blind pensioners and others, and I would like in particular to join in supporting the appeal which the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) made last night on behalf of veterans of the first world war who saw service only in the United Kingdom and who as a result are not eligible for war veterans' allowances. These are obvious questions, and questions to which immediate attention should be given by a government which professes to be representing the general interest of the people of Canada.
Someone has said that if capital and labour ever get together it will be "good night" to the rest of us, which recalls the original point I was making, namely that we find prices and wages going up in parts of the Canadian economy and remaining static in others. In these circumstances there is more truth than fiction in a statement of that kind. The price situation is, of course, giving rise to much discussion in western Canada concerning a fair price relationship. We hear a lot of talk among farmers' organizations about the necessity for parity. I think we can quite safely say that in regard to government intervention in economic matters the farmer has been the most neglected individual. Last spring we were sitting in on a hearing in connection with amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act and we were hearing evidence from Dr. Hope, who is the economist for the Canadian federation of agriculture. Someone-I have

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale forgotten which member it was, but it was one of the members from Saskatchewan- asked Dr. Hope this pointed question: "Do you, Dr. Hope, know of any country where the government does less for the farmer than does the Canadian government"? Dr. Hope's reply was very brief, yet very emphatic. It was: "No".
The agitation that goes on in the west as the farmers try to cope with the very rapid changes that are taking place in the economy is quite justified. A lot of it, perhaps, is not in touch with the realities of economics and there has been a divergency of opinion expressed from time to time; the organizations representing the farmers have not agreed as to what the best solution might be. But certainly, Mr. Speaker, something has to be done to stabilize the price position of the farmer more effectively if we are going to avoid some of the worst consequences to our agricultural industry. The Gordon commission deals with this question. I cannot refer to its report in any detail because I have not had time to read it fully but, briefly, the commission does refer to farm prices and makes recommendations concerning the activities of the Canadian wheat board and, no doubt, the government will be giving attention to some of these recommendations. On page 29 of the report in the chapter headed "Agriculture", paragraph 15, the report says:
We believe that the objective of a price support program for farmers should be roughly the same as that of unemployment assistance to industrial workers, namely, to mitigate distress due to economic fluctuations.
In paragraph 16 the report goes further with regard to this subject, and the concluding sentence says:
We believe that the determination of the support price on the advice of a full-time board would be preferable to the application of more or less automatic formulae.
These are specific recommendations made by the economists who were dealing with the problems.
The movement of people from the farms is one of the major difficulties. Dr. Baker, who has been conducting some research into agricultural matters in the province of Saskatchewan, says that the small farm has become obsolete on the prairies and that we are going to see a continuation of this movement of farmers away from the prairies. This is, of course, related to the problems of the price squeeze and surplus production. The danger point here is not that the farmers are leaving the farms-that is an inevitable process in a changing economy-but that the changeover may not be accomplished satisfactorily. I see, as I glance through the Gordon commission report, that in the year

1980, they mention, four out of every five of our citizens will be living in urban communities, which suggests that this trend from country to city will continue apace. But that is not the crux of the problem. The crux of the problem is: Where do they go and how do they get there? That is a matter to which this government has given absolutely no attention though it is one of the major difficulties which lie before us. The solution involves changes in educational policy-we shall be discussing that at length, Mr. Speaker, in this house in relation to improved grants to universities-it involves equitable distribution of industry across Canada rather than having it concentrated in two central provinces; it raises the old question of the decentralization of industry, and the government has hardly given that any consideration whatsoever.
This involves all the problems that arise when resettlement problems emerge in our economy. For example, with respect to the educational problem it has been pointed out to us on many occasions that we are not beginning to meet the need for new technicians in Canada. In a recent Citizen's Forum discussion on radio and television it was pointed out that we need immediately 100,000 new technicians. How are we going to produce them? We have two institutions devoted to this activity, the Ryerson Institute in Toronto and the Institute of Technology in the city of Calgary. They are capable of producing a relatively small number of technicians each year. In contrast, Russia has 1,500 technical schools.
This means that we are wasting the talents of our engineers by having them perform the functions of technicians when they should be devoting their better training to the functions of engineers. Someone has suggested that the proportion of technicians to engineers should be four to one. At the present time our position is the reverse: we have approximately three engineers for every technician. This situation is vitally related to the agricultural problem I have been discussing. If young people are moving from the farms in response to the changing economic pressures, if smaller farms are being absorbed in larger farms, certainly there is plenty of room for these displaced persons in our growing industrial activity, but the government must take some responsibility with respect to resettlement and retraining.
My time is rapidly coming to an end and rather than go farther with the matter of inequities in our national development I shall leave it on the basis of what I have said about agriculture. I could have gone further and discussed the industrial aspect. The two are closely related. After all, we are a national

economy and if changes take place in one segment we must make the necessary adjustments to restore a balance to the situation.
Donald Creighton, who has acquired a certain fame recently following the publication of his excellent biography of the life of Sir John A. Macdonald, Canada's first prime minister, made a speech to the anniversary banquet of the United Grain Growers in Calgary last November in which he put his finger on the nub of the matter with respect to the point I have been trying to make that there is an imbalance in development in Canada. At that time he said:
The farm leaders drove home the truth that a true national policy must be for the whole nation, for agriculture as well as for industry, and that the powers and resources of the state must be employed so as to distribute burdens and equalize opportunities over the nation and through all its classes and groups.
That, I think, Mr. Speaker, is an excellent summary of the approach that must be taken by the federal government during these changing times. The speech from the throne was utterly disappointing in this respect. I trust that the government, in any further proposals that it makes during this important session of parliament, will attempt to come to grips with the problem. Otherwise I am afraid the amendment to the speech from the throne moved by this group will come true very quickly in this country and it will be apparent that not only has the house lost confidence but that the people of Canada have also lost confidence in this administration.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robi-chaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The mover is well known to us all but we fellow New Brunswickers wish to express our appreciation of and gratitude for the manner in which our colleague from Gloucester county, New Brunswick, conducted himself during this debate. I believe his speech will be very well received by his constituents and by the people of the province of New Brunswick as a whole.
We met here on January 8 earlier this week at a time when a most serious and apparently unnecessary railway strike was affecting many parts of our great country. In my county, the county of Charlotte, we have no C.N.R. connections of any kind and this creates a more serious problem. Thous-
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart ands of tons of Minto coal go to the pulp mill at Woodland, Maine. Thousands of tons of Minto coal go to the cotton mills in Milltown in my own riding. Conleys, who export hundreds of thousands of pounds of lobster to the United States, are obliged to truck their product long distances under very difficult circumstances. Connors Brothers Limited are in the same position. Ganong Brothers Limited, candy manufacturers in St. Stephen, are in the same position. I have received telegrams from many people explaining the serious situation as supplies of coal are running very short at this time.
Unemployment directly and indirectly attributable to the strike is having a most serious effect in my constituency and in all parts of the maritime provinces. We must all acknowledge, however, that the city and port of Saint John will be harder hit than any other section of our province.
I had expected great things from the new leader of the official opposition (Mr. Die-fenbaker) when he spoke on this serious problem in the house a few days ago, and I was particularly sure that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) would come up with some constructive suggestions since his home city has been declared an area of serious emergency.

The attitude taken by these two hon. members, however, is one of fence-sitting, pussyfooting, petty politicians. In his remarks yesterday in this chamber the hon. member for Saint John-Albert mentioned a strike which took place a year ago at a sugar refinery in Saint John and immediately said with emphasis: Remember now, I am not taking sides. With respect to every other strike he mentioned he wanted to emphasize the fact that he did not want it forgotten that he was not taking sides. The same statement was made with respect to the present strike arid the difficulties we have had to contend with in our part of the country. In his remarks regarding the railway strike he was most careful not to commit himself in any way. When he resumed his seat I asked him a question. I did not interrupt while he was speaking. I said, as found at page 68 of Hansard:
I would like the hon. member to tell us, if he would, what he would suggest as a solution to the railway strike.

The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart
He answered:
The resignation of this government would be the best one

The resignation of the present government would only mean a 20 year delay so far as the Conservative party is concerned. That may be his solution to the problem but I know that most people in the maritime provinces would not be prepared to wait 20 years for a solution of this serious railway strike with which we are faced right now.

speechtext:
I do not think that is quite as silly as my friend to the left because I keep still when others are speaking. I think he might follow the same practice. It is quite obvious that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert left this serious matter in a way that would allow him to interpret his remarks in any manner he wished. If the hon. member for Saint John-Albert were asked by a C.P.R. employee what his views were, he could immediately change this whole situation to meet the need. If he were asked by the management of the C.P.R. what his views were in connection with the matter, again, if he would be honest, he would say, "I have said nothing". But I feel quite sure that his attitude in this regard will not be acceptable to his own home city of Saint John. I do not believe that they would be satisfied with the manner in which he has dealt with this matter.
I received telegrams from W. W. Macaulay, mayor of Saint John; Parker D. Mitchell, mayor of the city of Lancaster; and E. B. Ross, deputy mayor of St. Andrews; Charlotte county board of trade and other boards of trade. In every case these words were used: A state of emergency exists. We request you to act at once by urging the government to use their emergency powers. That is exactly what I did when I came to Ottawa. I urged upon the government the necessity of settling the strike as soon as possible, and that they use anything within their power to see that it was settled. I want the people in my constituency to know just where I stand in this regard. There is no pussy-footing on my part. I believe in being straightforward and speaking what you believe to be honest facts.
The telegrams I have received are all urgent ones. The people who are sending those telegrams are greatly alarmed over
[Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) .1

conditions there at this particular time. I believe that circumstances warrant members from the maritimes taking that stand and that action. However, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I am sorry to say, did not take a stand at any time during his remarks in this house. It was a case of sitting on the fence from start to finish. It may not offend many in his constituency, but I feel sure it will not be endorsed by too many either.
After his remarks in connection with tht strike, the hon. member went on to condemn the federal government for their lack of interest in the maritime provinces. At the same time he painted a most gloomy picture of our economic future. I have here an advertisement that appeared in his own Saint John Telegraph-Journal just six months ago. It was placed in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal by the Progressive Conservative Association of New Brunswick. It reads in part:
Premier Hugh John Flemming has announced a $20 million manganese refining industry for New 13 runs wick.
Attorney General West has announced the reopening of the mill at Marysville.
The Ministers of Agriculture and of Industry and Development have announced a new frozen food plant for Florenceville. Another one is in prospect for the city of Lancaster.
Hon. Mr. Fournier has announced the Flemming government will construct a new bridge at Edmundston. The new Limestone Bridge, in Victoria county, was officially opened Saturday.
The pulp and paper industry has announced plans for a huge five-year expansion program-a direct result of Hugh John Flemming's power development.
Wages are up more than 15 per cent since 1952. Construction is up 21 per cent in New Brunswick over last year-the second highest increase in all Canada.
The economy of the province was never better . . .
For three consecutive years, the Flemming government has reduced the net debt ...
I realize that when we reduce a net debt here we are bitterly criticized by those sitting in the official opposition. But I am proud of any government that has a surplus rather than a deficit. Surely a government that has a surplus, be it federal or provincial, does not need financial aid. When they boast of their surpluses, it is good indication to the people of this country that things are not too bad.
I might follow this up with the statement that on New Year's eve our premier came out with a statement in the same glowing terms as the one I have just read, indicating that conditions were very good in our province. At that time I am sure he did not ask for any assistance of any kind. That story that was told in June and the one that was told on New Year's eve is different from the story we

heard told here yesterday by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. He made no mention, it is true, of the fact that the federal expenditure in the province of New Brunswick during the past twelve months was more than double the total revenue of our provincial government. This federal government spent in my province in the last twelve months $130 million but we never hear any credit given to anyone in connection with it. At this point I may say that $20 million of the $50 million that we have as our total revenue comes as a contribution from this government. Two fifths of our total revenue in the province of New Brunswick comes directly from the federal government. 1 never hear a Conservative member ever give anyone any credit for that. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in my province we could not exist without that assistance we are receiving from the federal government. There was no mention of the fact that this $20 million is used to provide employment for the friends of the Conservative government, something which is true. We all know it. Only yesterday I received a report. It is from the editorial and information division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and it reads in part as follows:
. . . plans were outlined for a 1957 expenditure of about $3,500,000 to control the spruce budworm outbreak in northern New Brunswick.
This has been going on for several years. The federal government has never been hesitant in any way in making their contribution. I have yet to find one single circumstance where this government has ever refused to assist our provincial government when it had a legitimate case to place before it. I have searched the record and can find no case where assistance, when it was requested from the province of New Brunswick and where it was felt that the matter under consideration was beyond their financial capacity, was not provided. I also doubt that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert himself can find any such case. I have not been able to do so.
There is an article that appears in Maclean's magazine-a copy was sent to me yesterday- by Blair Fraser. It is headed "Backstage at Ottawa" and there are some extremely interesting remarks in that particular article. Under the subheading "Where can Ottawa spend Its Hoarded Half-Billion?" we find the following:
One region that leaps to mind when capital development is discussed is, of course, the Atlantic provinces-the maritimes and Newfoundland. Hundreds of millions in public funds have been spent or lent to develop other parts of Canada in recent years, with projects like the St. Lawrence seaway and the trans-Canada pipeline. Nothing proportionate has been done for the Atlantic region.
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart
Ottawa would like to correct this imbalance. Hon. Robert H. Winters is Minister of Public Works as well as M.P. for Lunenburg, N.S., and a devoted maritimer.
That is something we all can confirm. The article continues:
He has repeatedly made, and Prime Minister St. Laurent has echoed, invitations to maritime spokesmen to bring to Ottawa any ideas they may have for development of their native land. The implication is that if money is all that's needed, that will be no obstacle.
So far there has been amazingly little response. New Brunswick has a hydro-electric project in mind but it presents serious engineering problems, as well as the doubt that a sound hydro project should need help anyway. Otherwise, a typical maritime reaction has been, "If Ottawa would make its suggestion more specific, we'd be delighted to discuss it''. The fact that Ottawa is inviting suggestions, not making them, is glossed over.
I think Blair Fraser made a true statement according to facts right there. He goes on to say that some plans have been proposed that are rather fantastic. We all know that. But as to any constructive plan that came from the province of New Brunswick that would help the province and the country, so far as federal funds are concerned I am confident that this government are prepared to go ahead and do what they can to improve conditions.
We must all admit, as New Brunswickers, that our retarded development in New Brunswick is caused by the serious lack of cheap electrical energy. We all know that. We can never hope to become an industrialized area until an abundance of electrical power at a reasonable cost can be developed. None of the projects now under construction or consideration can supply that power except the Passamaquoddy tidal power project. A survey has been undertaken jointly by the United States government and the Canadian government to determine whether this project is economically feasible. A full-scale investigation will get under way this spring. Today these engineers, whom I meet very often, are compiling information in their offices on both sides of the border that dates back 30 years. They hope to be able, by April 1, to get a full-scale investigation under way. It is my honest, sincere opinion that this is the only answer to our economic problems in New Brunswick. It is on this project that I pin my faith, and it is on this project that federal assistance will be required. It is on this project that federal assistance will be provided if the investigation proves the project is a sound one from an economic standpoint.
Again, I would wish to emphasize the fact that an abundance of cheap power is the only answer to our problem in New Brunswick. As Blair Fraser quite rightly said, some of the plans that have been proposed

The Address-Mr. Knowles whereby federal financial assistance would be required are pretty fantastic. Any assistance from the federal government should have long-term benefits, not just a flash in the pan. Let us hold this ace in the hole until we have the answer with regard to the Passamaquoddy project because that is the only source in New Brunswick, or in that area that I know of, where a great block of power might be provided. I have great faith in my own province, and I have faith in all the maritime provinces. If we wish to improve our standard of living and create an environment which will induce the young men and women to stay there with us, we must take full advantage of the bountiful resources God has provided for us. If all the citizens of the maritime provinces would place less emphasis on complaining and criticism and give more serious thought to constructive contributions, we might look to the future with a much more enthusiastic attitude. Criticism, as we listen to it here, and complaint without constructive suggestions, will never build a bigger and better maritimes which is the goal we all hope we may be able to achieve.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Members of this group, Mr. Speaker, are earnestly hoping that a settlement of the strike on the Canadian Pacific Railway will be reached today. In fact, we hope it might be reached at any moment, certainly within a few hours. We have felt right from the start that the only reason the strike came about was because the Canadian Pacific Railway insisted on injecting an issue into its negotiations with the firemen which should not have been raised at all, namely an issue relating to the safety of railway operations. I shall have something more to say about that in a moment.
May I at this point add the comment that we believe it has become clear to many more members of the house than was the case at the start, and has become clear to large sections of the public, that it is the intransigence of the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway which was responsible not only for the strike in the first place but is responsible for the delay in its settlement. The proposal the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has made to both sides for a temporary agreement similar to that made between the brotherhood and the Canadian National Railways is in line to a large extent with the proposals made earlier by the Canadian Labour Congress and supported by the union. It is also in line with the first proposal that we in this group made in a press release which we gave out on January 8. It is obvious, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal made by the Prime Minister is not only

one that commends itself to this house as reasonable, but it obviously commends itself to the men who are affected. Indeed, a report in this morning's Montreal Gazette says that Mr. Jodoin has stated that the Prime Minister's statements and suggestions were very acceptable to the Canadian Labour Congress and to the brotherhood. This seems to make it quite clear to all who may want to look at this matter objectively that it is the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway which is holding out on the very fair proposals made to both sides by the government. Any further continuing of the strike is, therefore, the responsibility of the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We hope that there will soon be agreement to the proposal made by the government so that the strike may be settled and the operation of the railway resumed.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that in the view of the members of this group the strike came about only because in the midst of negotiations on wages, working conditions and other matters, the Canadian Pacific sought to introduce an extraneous matter, namely the proposal to do away with firemen on diesel locomotives in yard and freight service regardless of the effect of such a change on the safety of railway operations. We feel that a false picture of this proposed change has been given, largely through the publicity channels of the Canadian Pacific Railways, as to what it meant. The Canadian Pacific Railway has tried to play up the fact that on diesel locomotives there is no need for firing, as such, as used to be the case on steam locomotives. The Canadian Pacific Railway has overlooked the other functions of the person known as fireman on diesel locomotives. Gradually, as this matter has been discussed, and as attention has been paid to it because of the fact a strike was in progress, people are beginning to realize that on modern diesel locomotives with modern lengthy trains travelling at high speeds, there are many other functions to perform that have taken the place of the actual firing that used to be the main task of the fireman.
Not only has the publicity which the C.P.R. has been able to get for its side of the case played up the fact that there is no actual firing necessary on the part of the fireman on a diesel locomotive, but it has played down the safety angle involved. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this attempt to draw attention to the fact that all the C.P.R. is asking for is the elimination of firemen on freight and yard diesels is an attempt to lull the public into a feeling of security in the knowledge that, for the moment at any rate, passenger trains will still have firemen on diesel locomotives. After

all, so far as the public is concerned, for the most part our experience is in travelling on passenger trains, and of course so long as the C.P.R. does not propose to take firemen off diesel locomotives hauling passenger trains the general public could have a certain sense of security.
I suggest there are two points which ought to be taken into consideration in regard to that phase of the matter. One is that the change in the diesel rule which Canadian Pacific Railway is asking for is an over-all blanket change. True, for the moment, the C.P.R. says it intends to take firemen off only yard and freight diesels, but the change in the rule is so comprehensive that it would be possible at any time for the C.P.R., under that new rule, to eliminate firemen from diesels hauling passenger trains as well.
Even apart from the question as to whether or not firemen would be taken off diesels hauling passenger trains, surely the Canadian Pacific Railway, the government, parliament and the public have a responsibility to the employees who operate freight trains. Even if they never take them off passenger diesels, the fact is that we have a responsibility to protect the life and limb of those who are operating freight trains. To us it is a case of a callous disregard of the rights of workers for the Canadian Pacific Railway to assume that in the eyes of the public it is perfectly all right to have less of a safety factor on yard and freight trains than the public would expect to have on passenger trains.
During the negotiations, once this issue was raised, representations, of course, were made as best they could be made by the representatives of the brotherhood. I have had the privilege of looking over some of the evidence that was presented; I have had the privilege of seeing copies of scores of photographs that were shown to the board indicating the difficulties of operating diesel locomotives in yard service. Those photographs which were presented to the conciliation board show instance after instance where the view of the engineer on the right side of a diesel locomotive is completely obstructed so far as the situation on the left side of the train is concerned, to the increase of danger to the employees who have just as much right to protection by the C.P.R., protection by parliament and protection by the public as have passengers who ride on the trains operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
There is also the factor, Mr. Speaker, that if you step by step do away with the firemen on diesel locomotives, and if you increase the dieselization of our railways, the 82715-9i
The Address-Mr. Knowles day will come when, with present engineers retiring and moving out of the picture, engineers will have to be trained without having had the prior experience of being firemen. I have had both correspondence and conversations with engineers as well as with firemen during the time this matter has been under discussion, and engineers have said to me that they would not want to become engineers without first of all having had the experience of being firemen. It is one thing to train a person as to the actual techniques of operating a modern locomotive; it is another thing to have the experience of being put through as a sort of co-engineer during the years that one is a fireman. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we feel that this whole safety factor is one that has not been sufficiently publicized during the time this matter has been in dispute. It has not been sufficiently appreciated by the Canadian Pacific Railway; indeed, we think it was not sufficiently appreciated by the conciliation board. In our view, it should not have been thrown into these negotiations at all. If the Canadian Pacific Railway had not come along after the negotiations were started and thrown in this issue I am sure that the other matters that were being negotiated by the parties could have been settled and we would not have had a strike at all.
The day has to come, Mr. Speaker, when an organization such as the Canadian Pacific Railway must realize its responsibility in matters of labour relations. Parliament does its best to regulate labour relations by legislation such as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act; but even after the legislation has been passed, even after the best possible legislation has been passed, harmonious labour relations will depend on good will on the part of both sides. This whole story of the relations between the Canadian Pacific Railway and its firemen is an example, in our view, of a high-handed attitude toward labour, of a disregard for the safety factor and a willingness to trifle with the safety of workers and the public in order to try to beat down the wage and other demands of the union. We think the Canadian Pacific Railway must yet learn the lesson that in addition to good labour legislation we need the type of management that recognizes its responsibility to all sections of the public, including its responsibility to the employees who work for a company such as the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Others have already spoken on this matter on behalf of this group, and all of us who speak are expressing the views of all members of this group. In the remarks that have been made it has been pointed out-but perhaps it

The Address-Mr. Knowles should be pointed out again-that the attempt of the Canadian Pacific Railway and particularly the attempt of its president, Mr. N. R. Crump, to rely on the fact that the conciliation board agreed to the elimination of firemen from yard and freight diesels is really not justified. After all, that board consisted of three members. The majority recommendation, signed by two members, was qualified by certain doubts. The third member, Senator Roebuck, made a very strong recommendation, a very strongly worded report, which he submitted to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), opposing outright the proposal to eliminate firemen from its locomotives. He went so far as to call upon the Canadian Pacific Railway to withdraw its ill-conceived proposal. He said that he was fortified in his position by what had been done by the Canadian National Railways and by what had been done by all the railways in the United States. He also cited his experience as a lawyer when on occasions he had had to defend engineers against charges of manslaughter. On the basis of that experience, he pointed out that it is an extremely onerous responsibility that is placed on engineers, and, in his view, no engineer should be asked to operate any locomotive, passenger, freight or yard, without having a co-engineer, or a fireman, as the second person in the cab.
There has been some discussion about the time when the head trainman rides in the cab, and it has been said that he provides the second person but, as Senator Roebuck and others have pointed out, the responsibilities of the head brakeman or the head trainman are of a totally different nature. He is concerned with the train itself, and the work that he has to do when the train is stopped. His whole responsibility, and his whole training, detract from the possibility of his taking care of the safety factors which the fireman is in a position to assume. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we feel satisfied the time has come when the public has begun to get a little different picture of this from what was the case at the start. First, it was thought by many just that here was a group of people trying to hold on to their jobs. Any of us who have had connections with trade unions know that the trade union movement accepts and welcomes technological changes. It does its best to protect the rights of workers as changes take place; but to suggest that this is only an attempt to stop progress on the part of the union is to be completely false to the approach of the trade union movement generally. Indeed, the very thing that we are talking

about, namely, dieselization has already displaced many other workers, machinists, and so on, across this country. There has not been any strike over that, much as it has done by way of dislocating many people because, in the other instances, the safety factor was not involved, as it is in this situation.
We are glad of one other thing, Mr. Speaker, in this whole story. So far there has been no attempt on the part of the government to repeat the performance of 1950. There have been those who have spoken in this debate who have come pretty close to the suggestion that the government should use its power-I was not sure of what the last speaker had in mind-to get the railways running again, even if it meant forcing the men back to work. We feel that real damage was done to collective bargaining and to labour-management relations on the railways when, in 1950, the government called upon parliament to pass a bill which we opposed, that included compulsory arbitration. To the extent that that has not been done at this time-and I hope the government will stay with its refusal to resort to compulsory arbitration-to that extent some of the damage that was done in 1950 is being undone. As a matter of fact, I think Mr. Crump assumed right from the start he had nothing to worry about, that the government which had put the men back to work by act of parliament in 1950 would do it again, that the government would not permit a railway strike to go on and so all he had to do was take his position, unreasonable as it was, and the government would bail him out.
I am glad the government has not asked parliament to do that and I hope other steps will be taken to reinstate the collective bargaining position that obtained on the railways prior to the strike of 1950. I say again, Mr. Speaker, not only is it necessary to have good labour legislation, not only is it necessary to have the good offices of the Department of Labour to mediate in situations like this, not only is it necessary to have well chosen conciliation boards, but harmonious labour relations depend upon goodwill and good faith on both sides and it is our feeling that the Canadian Pacific Railway management in this whole piece has been oblivious to the rights of the men concerned, has been oblivious to the safety factor not just as it affects the general public but as it affects even a few of its employees. We feel, as Senator Roebuck says, that the whole proposal should be withdrawn and that there should be no further attempt to reduce the safety of railway operation by eliminating

The Address-Mr. Knowles
the firemen from locomotives on any operation be it passenger, freight or yard service. That is our position on this important issue.
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two other matters about which I would like to say a few words at this time. First of all, I wish to refer once again to the question of the old age pension. I am delighted that this subject has been mentioned by hon. members who have spoken in this debate in all parts of the house. The tragedy is that it was not mentioned in the speech from the throne.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that if it had been possible to take a poll of public opinion prior to the reading of the speech from the throne it would have been pretty generally agreed that that speech would include a forecast of an increase in the old age pension. Certainly last year when the government was under fire during the pipe line debate, under fire not only here but in the press and suffering considerable discredit across the country, there were strong rumours to the effect that one of the ways in which the government would attempt to retrieve its position would be by bringing in improvements in social legislation at this session, one of them to be an increase in the old age pension.
Lo and behold, this year the government apparently thinks it has nothing to worry about, that it has the election in the bag. It may have another think coming. But because it thinks that way the government has brought down a speech from the throne with a few things contained in it that are acceptable and uncontentious but which contains nothing at all that comes to grips with the basic problems facing our people, such as the plight of our senior citizens.
It is well and good, Mr. Speaker, to boast about our buoyant economy and it is fine to talk about the great prosperity that exists in the country but the more our economy is buoyed up and the more prosperous the country is as a whole, the more tragic becomes the position of those who are on fixed incomes and particularly those who are on low fixed incomes.
This figure of $40 a month which is presently being paid under federal legislation both to those in receipt of old age security and those in receipt of old age assistance, as well as to the blind and the totally disabled, was set back in 1949. At that time the gross national production of this country was $16.4 billion a year. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if we have been able to increase our gross national production since 1949 it is only decent and proper that we should give to our old age pensioners an increase in what we pay them proportionate to the increase in our gross national production.
This year the gross national product may be $29 or $30 billion a year. If it is $29 billion that will be an increase of 77 per cent over what it was in 1949. If it is $30 billion that will be an increase of 82 per cent over what it was in 1949. The 77 per cent increase would call for an increase in the old age pension to $70 a month. The 82 per cent increase would call for an increase in the pension to $72 a month.
There was a time when to speak of figures like that for old age pension would have seemed outlandish but what the government does not seem to know is that Canadians generally have moved forward to the position that an old age pension should no longer be just an amount of money to keep a person barely alive but rather that an old age pension should be one of the rights of citizenship, should be one way of enabling our older people who have helped to build up the country to live in dignified and decent retirement and enjoy some of the wealth that the country is then producing because of what they have done.
We need-the country has it, it is the government that needs it-a new concept of the old age pension. The government should realize that it should be not just an existence allowance but rather the right to share in the wealth of the country at any given time. This party at its last national convention held in Winnipeg last August went on record urging that the old age pension be increased to not less than $65 a month and that it be payable without a means test from age 65.
I noticed that one Liberal across the way went out on a limb in expressing the opinion that the old age pension should be increased by $10 to $50 a month. In the light of the increase in our gross national product an increase of $10 a month would surely be very niggardly. We say that in the light of Canada's present increased prosperity and in the light of the suffering and needs of these people the pension should be increased to not less than $65 a month, and that these other figures I have given should be borne in mind for surely all Canadians are entitled to share in our gross national product.
Speaking of the gross national product it seems to be the popular thing today to refer to the Gordon report, preliminary copies of which reached us yesterday. I note in the report that if the conditions the board indicates are met it is expected that by 1980 the gross national product of Canada will reach the figure of $76 billion a year. I think it would not be improper for me to carry forward the percentage figuring I was doing a moment ago. If we do achieve a gross national product of $76 billion a year
134	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles by 1980 that will represent an increase of 360 per cent over the $16.4 billion that obtained in 1949. If the old age pension were to be increased in proportion thereto it should be raised by 1980 to $184 a month.
Now I say again to hon. members, do not laugh at this kind of figure just because some hon. members were brought up in the days when the old age pension was $20 a month, barely enough to keep body and soul together. The old age pension has a purpose different from mere existence. Its purpose is to recognize what older people have done for the country and to give them their share of a decent life as we would do in any ordinary decent family.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, we are going to have to reconsider this whole question. It seems to me that what we need in relation to old age pensions is not only the universal plan we have that pays a flat amount to all our people but in addition to that we need something in the nature of the national industrial pension plan which has been proposed by the Canadian Labour Congress and the sooner we come to grips with this issue at the parliamentary level the better it will be for this country as a whole. There is really not very much in the speech from the throne for this session. I suppose that after the debate on the address is over a couple of weeks would be sufficient to clean up all the legislation set out in the speech from the throne. Maybe that is what the government intends, that we will be here for a couple of weeks and then go home for the election, but there are indications that we are going to stay here until close to Easter.
Therefore I suggest that if the government is not prepared on its own to bring in a substantial increase in the old age pension it should do what was done in 1950 and appoint immediately a special committee of this house to consider the whole question of old age pensions to see if what some of us are saying is not the proper course, namely that the universal pension now paid under old age security should be increased to a figure of $65 a month or more and made payable at age 65 years, and that in addition to that there should be established a comprehensive national industrial pension plan so that all pension plans of workers and others in the country could be integrated on a contributory basis, so the funds invested in that way could be controlled for the good of the country, and so we might look forward to the provision of decent and dignified retirement for our senior citizens instead of the mere pittance that they now have to keep themselves alive.

This issue is one of deep importance. I feel, as do many members of this group, that it is a matter of great regret that the government has shown by its barren speech from the throne that it thinks it has the election won so why disturb it; that they just have to sit back and let things go their own way. They may have to have another thought about that, but even if it were true that the government stands to win the next election, what sort of leadership is it to sit back and do nothing because you are not being pressed by political considerations. If that is what the government wants, if it wants pressure and prodding and the fear of defeat in order to provide action on this issue we will do our best to give that to them because we believe the people of Canada are entitled at this time to a substantial increase in the old age pension that is now paid and that they are entitled at this time to a consideration of this whole question proposed by Mr. Jodoin and the Canadian Labour Congress of a national pension plan which my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and others of us have been proposing in this house for many years.
I urge this question of old age pensions as strongly as I can because it seems to me that the lethargy of the government, feeling that it did something back in 1950 and 1951, does not meet the wishes or the thinking of the Canadian people. This concerns not onlj the senior citizens themselves but younger people who have concern for them and who are thinking about their own futures. They realize that when a country can boast of a $29 billion or $30 billion gross national production, when a country is pictured in the Gordon report as going to have a production of $76 billion by 1980, it is not being decent, it is not being sensible, it is not being humane when it gives such a short end of the stick to our senior citizens.
Not only is the government showing its indifference to the wishes and needs of the people by its failure to act in this field of old age pensions, it is also highly noticeable, as my leader and others have pointed out, that there is no reference in the speech from the throne to the question of health insurance. Hon. members will recall the great fanfare we had last year. Of course the leader of that fanfare is not here at the moment to keep it going but I understand he will be back in a few days. I refer to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). A year ago we had a conference attended by the provincial representatives which the minister said was one of the finest conferences they had ever had.

He sat back for a while and then a proposition was made but attached to the proposition was a condition that it would be put into effect only if a substantial majority of the provinces representing a substantial majority of the population of Canada agreed to it.
That meant that there had to be agreement by six provinces, and that either Ontario or Quebec had to be included in those six. We pointed out at the time that the plan, although a step in the right direction, and despite of the shortcomings of its coverage, did not make a sufficiently attractive offer to the provinces to ensure that six would agree. We have had a year and only three, namely the three western provinces, have agreed to the plan. My own province of Manitoba, which has the only Liberal government in the country west of those which border on the Atlantic ocean, has virtually said that it will not have anything to do with the plan. No Liberal government in Canada has shown any interest in it to the point of indicating it would agree. No other governments have come in and it begins to look as though the plan is virtually dead.
I say to the government that if they were acting in good faith a year ago when they were talking about health insurance they should realize that a year having gone by with only three provinces agreeing the time has come when they should review the proposition and improve and revise the offer so that they can get six provinces to agree. In fact, that is what I looked for in the speech from the throne. After all an election is coming and a pre-election speech from the throne usually pays some attention to the wishes and needs of the Canadian people.
Here is a field, like that of old age pensions, where the needs of the Canadian people are very great, particularly so just now when hospital and medical costs are going up and when increases are reflected in increases in the Blue Cross and other medical plan payments. Things are getting to the point where despite our prosperity, of which the government of this country boasts, the basic care of health is something that is being rationed to our people by their purse. We are not getting the full advantage of medical science or of the money being spent on hospital construction and in other ways.
It all awaits a plan to make these things financially possible for the Canadian people. It all awaits a plan of health insurance. We feel that any plan of health insurance should be comprehensive and include not only hospitalization but medical, dental and optical care. It should include sickness benefits when the bread-winner is out of work. That is our
The Address-Mr. Knowles objective. Nevertheless, we admit that it is a good thing to get started. On that basis we admit that the proposal made by the government last year for national hospitalization insurance was a step in the right direction.
I am sure that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) who is paying me the honour of listening to what I am saying, will agree with me that it is now obvious that the terms of last year's proposal were not attractive enough. A sufficient number of provinces have not agreed. If there is any sincerity and validity to the 38-year old interest in health insurance evinced by the Liberal party that should be indicated now by increasing the offer to the provinces so that six of them will come in and we can get health insurance started.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.
