I am sure we all hope such an announcement will be made before the house rises at six o'clock. Indeed, if a settlement is not reached very soon on what I might call the basis of the first point in our proposal of the other day, namely, a request to both parties that they resume operations leaving the diesel question to be settled later, the government may have to consider the second point of our proposal, namely taking over the C.P.R. and running it pending a settlement of that issue. Nevertheless, it is our hope that an announcement of a settlement can, as I said before, be made by the government before the house rises at six o'clock tonight.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just one further word on the two other subjects which I raised before lunch. It is our view and, we believe it is the opinion of a vast number of Canadian people, that action should be taken by the government at this session of parliament on the old age pension question and on the matter of national health insurance. We believe that the old age pension should be raised substantially now. We believe a national health insurance plan with provision for provincial participation should be put on the statute books now. We

The Address-Mr. Batten contend, indeed, that if the government fails in its responsibility in these two matters it should be dealt with by the people of Canada at election time giving it the treatment which such an irresponsible government should be given.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset join with the others who have preceded me in extending heartiest congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have ably discharged their duties with, I am sure, credit to themselves and to the constituencies which they represent.
There are in the speech from the throne a number of items in which I am particularly interested but on this occasion I am going to confine my remarks to just one. May I refer to that section of the speech from the throne which deals with agriculture? It is proposed to recommend in the Senate the establishment of a committee to consider what should be done to make better use of land for agriculture and thus to contribute more effectively to the improvement of agricultural production and the incomes of those connected with it. I would hope that any such committee would take the view that the approach in any region should be made not only with a view to the percentage importance to the national income but also with regard to the value of the industry as a source of employment and to its importance in the economy of the region under study. I say that for this reason: the farm income of Newfoundland would be a very small percentage of the total farm income of all the provinces of Canada and the result is that if we were to approach the problem of agriculture in Newfoundland and to give it only the importance, percentagewise, that it has in the total national economy it would not receive the attention it deserves in the general economy of the province of Newfoundland and, in particular, the importance of the industry to the various regions where agriculture is carried out in Newfoundland.
As everybody knows, Newfoundland is not an agricultural province. We, like other parts of Canada, have our limitations; for example, we have a limitation of climate- our climate may in some respects not be such as to enable us to produce certain agricultural products which are produced in other parts of Canada. Nevertheless the limitation placed upon agriculture in Newfoundland is not such as to prevent, for example, poultry enterprises, livestock farming and root vegetable growing being carried out successfully.


We also have limitations with regard to soil. Our soil is mainly of the mineral variety. It has a high acid content and a low content of organic material. We do have some alluvial soil, found mostly in the areas surrounding the mouths of the rivers, particularly those flowing into the gulf of St. Lawrence. We have no large areas of heavy clay such as are found in some of the other provinces of Canada but there are, nevertheless, considerable areas, usually consisting of small acreages, where farming is being carried out very successfully, and these limitations of climate and soil to which I have referred are not such as would prohibit poultry enterprises, livestock farming and root vegetable farming. I believe the potential is such as to warrant sufficient attention to make it play a more important part in' the economy of the province than it has in the past or does now at the present time in its expanded state.
The growth of agriculture in Newfoundland has been very slow. In the early days following colonization, I believe I may say, no encouragement was given to (farming; it might even be more correct to say that settlement and the cultivation of the land were actually prohibited. It was not until 1813- over two centuries after the first days of colonization-that permission to lease land for agricultural purposes was granted, and it was only granted then on 30-year leases and on payment of an annual rent. Nine years later these rents were abolished and in 1825 Governor Cochrane, the first resident governor of Newfoundland, gave some impetus to agriculture within the province. However, it was not until 1878 that the government of Newfoundland formally identified itself with the development of agriculture.
There were other factors too which hindered the growth of agriculture in the island. First, the early settlers were fishermen accustomed to the ways of the sea. They were not farmers. Secondly, fishing was a very attractive industry while farming was a very unattractive industry. Lack of roads and large rivers on the coast where most of the settlement took place meant that most of the interior was inaccessible. Thus, for those who came to settle there it was necessary to have as soon as possible a stable export commodity. That stable export commodity could be found in the fishing industry very easily; it was unlikely to be found in the farming industry as it existed in Newfoundland at that time. Fishermen gradually recognized the importance of farming in their own economy and gradually a system of supplementary farming was developed. This means, of course, that attention was

The Address-Mr. Batten
given to the farming industry when the returns from the fishing industry were poor. No attention was given to the farming industry when the returns from the fishing industry were good. The history of supplementary farming has been that it is not a very consistent effort. In more recent times the development of other industries within the province has taken labour from not only the farming industry but also the fishing industry.
In the report of the royal commission on farming published in 1955 it is pointed out on page 29 that in 1921 there were 38,206 people engaged in some form of farming but only 3,227 of those were full-time farmers. In 1935 there were 39,808 people engaged in farming but only 4,226 were engaged in farming as a full-time occupation. In 1945 35,574 people were engaged in cultivating the land but only 2,809 of those could be considered as full-time farmers.
Since 1949 there has been a very marked and pronounced expansion in some types of farming and particularly in the poultry enterprise. I would say there are many reasons for this. One would be first of all the small amount of land required by this particular industry. Second, there was the growth of larger areas which served as markets for the produce from the poultry enterprise. Third, there was the improvement in the general welfare which enabled people to buy the produce of the poultry industry.
But one thing that had a very great effect upon the development of the poultry enterprise in Newfoundland was the feed grain freight assistance policy initiated by this government in 1941. If I may digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, over the last few years we have experienced successive increases in freight rates and these successive increases in freight rates are beginning to be felt very keenly both in the commercial and industrial life in Newfoundland. We, because we live on the fringe of this great country, have a long haul, and when there is an increase in freight rate based percentagewise it means that because we have a longer haul and therefore a larger amount of freight to be paid the people of Newfoundland will pay a higher increase than anybody else east of Ottawa.
On the other hand, we do not, for example, have the road systems and the trucking concerns that would enable us to offer any alternative to the present carriers now operating in Newfoundland which are, of course, the C.N.R. operating their rail line from Port aux Basques to St. John's and also operating the steamship services around the coast of Newfoundland. We have no alternative to these 82715-10
carriers and therefore whatever increase there happens to be in freight rates we just have to pay the shot.
I should like for a moment to look at the freight rates from, for example, the lakehead to one or two rail points in Newfoundland, and I take this particular route because I want to return to feed grains. Before January 30, 1956, a hundred-weight of freight shipped from the lakehead to Toronto cost 55 cents. On January 1 of this year, owing to the increase amounting to 11 per cent, people in Toronto are now paying 61 cents or an increase of 6 cents. This, as I said before, results from the 7 per cent increase authorized on June 18, 1956 by the board of transport commissioners which came into effect on July 3, and also by reason of the authority given by the board to the railways on December 17 for a further increase of 4 per cent, thus bringing freight rates to a level 11 per cent above those which prevailed on June 30, 1956. As a result of this, as I have just said, there is an increase of 6 cents per hundredweight or $1.20 per ton from the lakehead to Toronto.
Coming down to Corner Brook, Newfoundland, the increase is from $1.17 to $1.30 per hundredweight or 13 cents. Per ton the increase is from $23.40 to $26, or an increase of $2,60. In other words, the increase in the freight rate for a ton of freight from the lakehead to Corner Brook, Newfoundland, is three times as much as the increase in the case of the province of Ontario or near rail points in the province of Quebec.
These increases in freight rates become more significant when we are dealing with commodities which have been given some freight assistance as in the case of feed grains, for then the consignee must not only pay the increase in the freight rates based upon the freight but must also pay the increase based upon the percentage of the assistance. Let me give an example of exactly what I mean. Because of the feed grain freight assistance policy of the Department of Agriculture, all the maritime provinces, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, prior to June 30, 1956 received feed grains at a freight rate of $5 per ton to the consignee. The difference between the $5 and the actual cost of the freight was made up by this assistance policy.
But now with an 11 percent increase in the freight rate the freight rate on a ton of feed from the lakehead to Corner Brook, for example, has now been increased by $2.60 which means that we are now paying $7.60 where previously we paid $5. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the increase of 11 per

The Address-Mr. Nowlan cent in the freight rate has resulted in a 52 per cent increase in the actual freight paid by the consignee in Corner Brook. If we go farther along and take the town of St. John's we find that the recent increase of 11 per cent in freight rates has resulted in an actual increase to the consignee of 64 per cent.
I should like to say at this time that these feed grains are very important to Newfoundland not only in the poultry enterprise but also in the livestock industry and the lumber industry. May I respectfully suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) at this time that consideration be given to some form of corrective adjustment so that the inequalities now existing will not retard expansion in the industries concerned and so that they may continue to enjoy the advantages which they have received as a result of this policy.

Mr. Speaker, as usual at the commencement of a new speech in this debate one pays tribute to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Such tributes may sometimes be conventional but they are usually and almost always sincere. They certainly are in this case because I am sure the two hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the address in this debate acquitted themselves with distinction and deserve the congratulations of all members of the house.
This has been a rather unique session. In the few short days that we have been here, overhanging the atmosphere of the house, of course, has been the paramount national question of the settlement of the railway strike. In addition, we have seen certain historical events moving before us. We have seen the resignation as a member of this house of the leader of the political party to which I belong, one who I am sure all members will agree has served this house and his country with distinction, and the house is the poorer because of his resignation.
We have also read of the resignation of the prime minister of the United Kingdom. Within the last 48 hours we have seen unveiled here a memorial to a former Conservative leader, a former prime minister of this country. Hence, in the few short hours in which we have been sitting here much of political history has been enacted or dramatized before our eyes. Personally, I am extremely happy to have seen this memorial unveiled. It is something which I had advocated for some years in the past as, shall I say, the political descendant of


the gentleman in question. In the days in which he represented a Nova Scotia constituency redistribution had not taken the toll of the constituency which it since has taken and he was the member for Kings county which is part of my own constituency today.
I am sure all the people of Nova Scotia, particularly those of that county, appreciate the tributes which were paid to his memory and the memorial which has been erected to him on the grounds of this parliament building, where the services which he rendered to this country with such great distinction will be memorialized and, we trust, perpetuated, subject to atomic bombs, at least within the memory and the lifetime of any of us who are now serving in parliament or have any connection with the government of Canada.
As I said a moment ago, the one matter which is uppermost in our minds is the question of the strike. If it were not for that matter I do not think I would have trespassed on the time of the house on this occasion. There are many things which one could discuss. Perhaps it is rather discouraging, Mr. Speaker, when one goes back to the speeches that one has made on a similar occasion during the last six or seven years, to find how many matters one has suggested and to note that some of those problems are still before us.
However, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has stated, we are all hopeful that the strike will be settled within the next few hours. We have been waiting in anticipation of an announcement to that effect. The hon. member suggested that there was a great deal of intransigence on one side, namely, on the side of the management of the C.P.R. Naturally, we would not expect him to attribute any intransigence to the firemen. I think one can say quite fairly that his speech was, to a large extent, an apologia for the firemen's union or brotherhood. I have had the privilege and the pleasure of knowing many of those members personally. I come from a constituency which is served entirely by a wholly-owned subsidiary of the C.P.R. I know many of those firemen. No finer citizens live in this country than the firemen in the employment of the Dominion Atlantic Railway and, I presume, generally in the employment of the C.P.R. We know that they are not the type who would wilfully promote trouble or wilfully attempt to wreck the economy of this country. Yet there is at stake a larger issue than that. We have that constituency today,

The Address-Mr. Nowlan
as I said, which is wholly served by this C.P.R. subsidiary, with the exception of one station, completely tied up, with not a wheel moving on the railroads except in the town of Middleton where a branch of the Canadian National runs from the constituency of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) right across into the valley and possibly as a last resort fuel and supplies could be brought in there to avert a disaster.
But at the moment we are dependent to a substantial extent on the apple industry. Having harvested the apple crop, having had it packed, having had negotiations with the government of Great Britain, many of our shipments having been made to Great Britain but many to be made in January and February and that is the situation now. We have tens of thousands of boxes of apples headed to the British market which we cannot move. I can understand the complaints, the worries of our friends from the west where a similar situation confronts the wheat grower; but at least wheat will keep. Under the aegis of this government they have had to keep the wheat for a long while now and they will probably have to keep it for a while longer yet. But you cannot keep apples indefinitely. Steamship space has been bought. Steamers have been coming into Halifax with space booked which we could not fill.
You cannot truck those apples because, with subzero temperatures, it is impossible to transport them in that way at this time of year. They must go in reefer cars. The reefer cars are immobilized. The whole fruit industry of the valley is affected, I was going to say, but of course not all of it is affected because substantial marketings were made in October, November and December. However, a substantial part of it is now completely tied up. If these apples cannot be moved within the next few days the fruit industry will suffer as bad a blow as it suffered last year because of the glut, when the market went completely to pieces and apples could not be sold. Hence our people down there feel that this government must exercise leadership in this matter and must achieve a solution and do so rapidly.
If my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is correct when he says there is intransigence on the one side, may I say in parenthesis that I have been involved in litigation and in disputes for a period of thirty years and I have never seen any one side have a monopoly on intransigence. Usually it is divided between the two sides to a certain extent. But if there is intransigence it is the duty of this government to solve the problem and to deal with it and 82715-10i
not to wait idly by piously hoping that something will happen whereby it will be unnecessary to take any action whatsoever.
I was brought up in a pioneering economy. I was born away out in the rural area of Digby county. As a little boy I used to go out to the sugar grove with my mother where they were boiling maple sap and making it into maple sugar. I remember her instructing me as to how it should be done. You had to get the syrup to a certain temperature. You had to get it hot enough and yet you had to have the snow cold enough so that when you brought the two together you could get a fusion of some kind and thereby you could manufacture maple sugar. I sometimes think this government has been waiting idly by, hoping that the temperature would get hot enough on the outside with public opinion and yet get cold enough on the inside so that by simply standing by and waiting they may jell something into maple syrup or maple sugar and thereby achieve settlement of the strike. That, Mr. Speaker, is not national leadership.
At least in so far as the part of the country from which I come is concerned, I could bring to this house and could read them to you, if you would permit me to do so, a stack of telegrams-forty or fifty of them- from boards of trade, mayors of towns, gentlemen who are well known to the Minister of Public Works, all saying one thing. They did not say what the hon. member for Charlotte read. Apparently they have more confidence in him as a member than my constituents have in me because he told us this morning that the telegrams told him to do something. My telegrams said: Tell the government to do something; we want the government to do something and that is what we need. If the prognostications are correct, and if within the next few hours a settlement can be negotiated, well and good. But if it cannot be negotiated, the economy of this country, at least that of the part of the country from which I come, will be injured. I have spoken particularly of the apple industry and the same thing could be said of the scallop fishermen. This is their season. This is the season in which scallops are being brought ashore every day. What can they do with them? Under normal circumstances they could perhaps run them across the bay of Fundy in their boats and ship them from Saint John. But as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) pointed out yesterday, Saint John is tied up. If they are going to ship them out of there, they have got to send them on ships to Saint John, Moncton and around a circuitous

The Address-Mr. Nowlan route into the markets of New England, Quebec or Ontario. The whole industry of that area has been brought to a full stop. The gypsum plant just outside my constituency had 800 men laid off because gypsum is moved by rail to the shipping point and there is no rail transportation. One could go on and on. I know this is the common story in many constituencies in this country, but I think perhaps we are harder hit because of our dependence upon this one railroad.
Wherever the fault may be, I have found the management of that company has always been considerate and has been desirous of serving the public interest. I know, too, that the employees are amongst the better citizens we have in this country. You cannot tell me, sir, that with action, with leadership, and if necessary some pressure, you could not achieve a result whereby this railroad could be put back into operation in the very near future. If it is not, then we are going to suffer an economic blow which will have repercussions for many years to come, and certainly it is going to have repercussions in the political field within the next few months.
In the particular area from which I come-[DOT] perhaps that is why we are more impatient in these matters-for weeks and months last summer and last fall we suffered a strike tying up the steamship system of the C.P.R. Wherever the intransigence may be now, there was no intransigence on the part of management in connection with that strike. Management was ready and willing at all times to start operation of that ship, but it could not be done. We have suffered two of these economic blows within the last nine months. In both of these cases it is felt that the government of this country has not given the leadership and the direction which is required. The people are asking for it, and I am urging it now. I say that the time has come when you had better stop waiting for the maple syrup to jell. You have to do some stirring yourself and not wait for the pot to boil over naturally as this government has been doing for the last eight or nine days. The sands have run out of the hourglass in so far as that thing is concerned.
Speaking of transportation, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of another matter that the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) was discussing a few moments ago, the feed grain subvention policy of this government and the effect of freight rates upon that. provinces as foreseen by this report? They refer to the difficulties and they say:

If it should turn out that there is not the necessary combination of resources in sufficient quantities to permit a substantial rise in living standards in the Atlantic region, generous assistance should be given to those people who might wish to move to other parts of Canada where there may be greater opportunities.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the address, I have to inform my colleagues that I shall not delay the passing of the address, but as the speech from the throne contains a paragraph on agriculture, and as my county consists almost entirely of farmers, it is my duty to thank, and to give credit to, the government for its position with regard to them.

Today, I would like to give an outline, as accurate as possible, of the conditions in which the farmers of my constituency find themselves. I say that should not he continued because we are blessed by Providence in this country with such great and valuable resources that any man's consistent arduous work could and should provide him with adequate returns . . .
I am convinced that some of the land in Eastern Canada that hard working Canadians are trying to use as farms should go back to forest and water conservation uses and those attempting to live on them resettled in more rewarding surroundings.
I therefore suggest that it should be the urgent business of all levels of government as well as private enterprise, both individual and co-operative to see to it that agricultural production keeps up with our increase in population and thus provides the farming population with a fair share of the national income.

Under this scheme, the federal government would share with the provinces the cost of programs of irrigation, of soil conservation, of land clearing and of the settlement of farmers living on submarginal lands.

Mr. St. Laurent stated his conviction that a certain proportion of eastern lands which Canadians have attempted to farm should be reforested or used in water conservation projects. For my part, I have repeatedly brought up this matter in the house, as I consider it of utmost importance for our farmers whose revenue would be inadequate if they could not make up for their agricultural deficits with income from their wood-lots. In my opinion, governments should seek the improvement of wood-lots.
There can be no doubt about the fact that our farmers' income is inadequate considering the amount of work they have to do. It seems to me that some wood lots should be added to the federal experimental farm and subjected to continuous study, in order that the forests which are adjuncts of the farms in my constituency, may be taken care of by our governments in the same way as agriculture.

May I make a recommendation? Federal and provincial authorities should co-operate in bringing wood lots under a forestry program so that all profitable wood lots may be used economically.

To realize how much our forests contribute to agriculture in the lower Quebec area, one need only read publication No. 890 of the federal

Department of Agriculture. This pamphlet deals with wood lots on Ontario farms and, at page 22, it is indicated that on the 162 farms which were thoroughly investigated, production reached a total value of $516 per farm.

Those experiments have been conducted in the province of Ontario with the co-operation of the federal Department of Agriculture and of the Ontario government. I hope similar experiments will be undertaken in my province to show how necessary it is to complement farming through the use of a wood lot in most regions.
Mr. Speaker, our farms in eastern Quebec need the shelter of wind-breaks. Our steep slopes should be reforested against disastrous gullying and erosion. Trees are also needed to prevent water from running too fast down steep slopes which separate the various high lands. Could not the government of Canada supply the experimental farm of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere with facilities for innovating in this field, because experimentation is not a matter for private enterprise but for governments, through their institutions, and our experimental farms are the sources of new achievements.
There is no better teaching than that acquired by looking at nature with our own eyes. Life is but the experience of others.
The establishment of a Senate committee to consider ways and means of making better use of land in eastern Quebec is an appropriate and courageous initiative on the part of the Prime Minister of Canada.
There is no doubt that certain areas should never have been farmed, for they could have yielded a higher return if they had been put to some other use.
A study of the development of agriculture in the lower St. Lawrence area indicates that the land was first cleared on the lower plateaux near the river, and then, with the increase in population, it was thought, with no idea of doing the wrong thing, that certain districts should be opened up which should have been left as they were or kept as wood lots. And conditions were made more difficult when parishes were founded and when certain institutions had been in existence for a long time. That is why I admire the spirited approach of the Canadian government in putting forward a program such as this.
Let us also keep in mind that a small bare rock on a farm presents a deplorable aspect to the traveller. On the other hand, a clump of variegated trees offers that same thirsty traveller a resting-place and brings revenue to the landowner.
It was I believe a prime minister of Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who said: "the heart

of a nation is in the depth of its forests; a people without forests is a dying people."

The Address-Mr. Hansell particularize. Let us take a look at the province of Saskatchewan from which the Leader of the Opposition comes. I will make this prediction. If he is elected-and he might be elected; it is conceivable to think that he might be elected-he will ne the only Conservative member coming back here from Saskatchewan after the next election. I will go to my own province of Alberta, where the Conservatives now have two seats. It is conceivable that they may return two members. It is also conceivable that their membership will be cut in half, because all they need to do is lose one member in order to achieve that result. However, I shall be a bit magnanimous in my prediction there. I will predict that after the next election they will not come back with any more than two members from Alberta. I will go to British Columbia and I will make this prediction. I will predict that they come back here with fewer members from British Columbia than they have now. I am not prepared to predict too much about Manitoba. However, I will predict that they will not come back with any greater number from the province of Manitoba. If my predictions prove to be correct and if they come back here with fewer members from west of the great lakes, then how on earth do they ever think they will form a government from the rest of Canada?

Your predictions are not
correct.

Mr. Speaker, once again I wish to say that I have the greatest respect for the new leader of the Conservative party. A little while ago I said that one of the best ways to destroy a political leader was to make him leader of the official opposition. Politics sometimes plays tricks. As to our own party, let me say this. I should like to see-and perhaps I shall-a little game of leap-frog that we sometimes play, whereby we leap over all the rest of the parties and leap from a third party to the government.
Oh, oh.

Of course I knew that somebody would smile at that statement, but let me tell hon. members that it has happened twice in Canada in recent years. In 1935 in the province of Alberta we did not have one legislator sitting in the legislature. We jumped from nothing. We leap-frogged over all the other parties and formed a government.
A few years later almost the same thing happened in British Columbia. We started with a nucleus of Social Credit support. When the campaign started out the C.C.F., the Liberals and the Conservatives were

The Address

Mr. Hansell fighting one another. The campaign got under way and they began to discover that there was quite a surge toward us, about three weeks to a month into the election campaign-a few weeks on-until about two weeks before election day, when they stopped fighting one another and trained their guns on us. Why should they do that if we were so inconsequential? However, they did it. We played leap-frog again and we jumped from nothing into the government. My friends can smile but it happened twice before. It is conceivable that it could happen once again.
I say that the leader of any opposition in any parliament in Canada is just like the proverbial coconut at the country fair: three chances for a dime or eight for a quarter. There he sits, the object of attack. Unless he can come clean with some definite alternative that can be presented to the people and that will capture their imagination, unless he has something to propose that will eclipse anything else, he goes down as a failure and the party remains in opposition.
One thing about which we are extremely proud in our party, Mr. Speaker, is that we have an alternative. Oh, you may not believe in it. You may say that it is all haywire. You may say that we are a lot of crackpots. But be that as it may, one thing you will not say is that we have not the ability to present an alternative in basic and fundamental policy; and when I speak of an alternative policy I do not mean a paint shop or a repair job. If something is fundamentally wrong with the combustion engine there is no use in saying we will change the tires. That procedure is no good, but that is the game our Conservative friends are playing. They say, "We will pursue a taxation policy, all right, but we will tax somebody else instead of somebody else. We will readjust the taxation. Oh, yes; we will pay bigger old age pensions, bigger this or bigger that." But if you ask them the question, "Where are you going to get the money from?" the answer you get is, "We will reduce our taxation."
Let us look at that picture. It is as plain as day. You must get the money if you are going to spend it. If it comes from taxation, then you must get more in taxation if you spend more money. It does not take even a grade 3 schoolboy to figure out that proposition. Have they any alternative suggestion? Have they any alternative basic policy?
The Social Credit organization for real political and economic democracy is, I may say, on the rise in Canada today. Two

provincial governments-those of Alberta and British Columbia-are Social Credit governments. These two governments have so administered the affairs of those provinces that they are two of the wealthiest, if not the wealthiest, provinces in Canada today. The people of the other provinces have taken note of this progress and have set up Social Credit organizations right across this country.
How did the wealth get there, in those two provinces?

The wealth has been there all the time, even with previous administrations. It is for that reason I say that when the Social Credit government took over in the hungry thirties things began to move because of wise policies.
Honest policies.

Yes, honest policies. Another reason for the spread of Social Credit throughout Canada is that once people realize the basic principles for which we stand they are gripped with a conviction that in Social Credit lies the great hope for a greater Canada with a happy and free people living in the economic security which our vast productive resources are able to give. Social Credit has developed in Canada into an active movement to free Canadians from the strangling dictatorship of the money power and political party machine rule, and to make the Canadian economy function in such a way as to give all people the economic justice which the enormous natural wealth of Canada is able to give. Social Credit is founded upon powerful and enduring principles which can never be destroyed.
We will settle for $25.
That old chestnut has been-
Roasted.
-bandied around a great deal. It has been roasted by old age. Don't ever believe that the old, old story of $25 per month cannot be answered. We have answered it over and over again.
The federal government can answer it, but not Social Credit.
Why doesn't it do it?

One of the great principles of Social Credit is that mankind was created to be free; that is an enduring principle. We claim that people are not to be regarded as the common herd to be pushed around at the whim of the masters. The very moment you do that you reduce mankind to the status of the beasts of the field.

The Address-Mr. Hansell
Why did you allow parliament to be pushed around during the session last spring? Why did you help push parliament around?
I should like to know why some people pushed Mr. Speaker around.
Ask the Minister of Finance; he is the man who did it.
Shame.
Supported by you.
The Tories do not like to be pushed around, that is the trouble.

Social Credit is based upon great moral principles and must not be regarded-this is one thing I want to point out-as it might be by some Canadian people who have a common conception that we are merely another political party.
Hear, hear.
Have you a monopoly on that principle?
Social Credit is a way of life.
So is bigamy.

It is more than merely a political party. If there had been a party in Canada that would have formulated great basic principles and brought into operation the monetary reform policies which we are advocating and which would solve the problems of Canada, there would have been no need for a Social Credit party. The reason we exist is that other parties refuse to bring about these monetary reform policies that we claim will be the means of solving the economic problems which face Canada today.
What Social Credit policies have you introduced in Alberta and British Columbia?
Oh, shut up.
That is the new way of life.

In the Social Credit movement we believe that all things were created for the benefit and progress of all mankind. We believe that man was given dominion over the whole earth, and that as he subdues it and through his expanding genius makes the earth yield an abundance of those good things of life, they should be distributed and made to bless all mankind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me dwell on that for a moment. Is it not the strangest thing in the world that an abundance in Canada today produces a problem for this government? That is a problem for which Social Credit has the answer, because our monetary policies are applied to the distribution of abundance. We have been advocating that for many, many years. It is one thing to which this present administration blind their eyes and regard abundances as catastrophes.

speechtext: No, no.

Well, they are not dealing
with them, anyway. Now, say "no, no" to that. They are frightened by an abundance; that is the strange thing. They fear some things that are good and proper.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: We consider we are blessed with abundance.
I am going to say this, that the present administration fears peace.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: That is ridiculous; you do not know what you are talking about.

It is not ridiculous. The one thing that is keeping the economy of this country going today is the cold war which necessitates the bolstering of our defences. If defence spending were to stop tomorrow we would be plunged into an abject depression. In that regard, this administration fear peace. This administration fear expansion, so they cut back credit and impose credit restrictions, thus preventing expansion.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

My leader gave an answer to that the other day. Read his speech; that is all you have to do. This present government fear progress. I will tell you what they fear. They fear automation. They have not the answer to automation.
Nobody has.
That is the very thing for which we do have the answer because all our active proposals are designed to meet a power age where men and women who labour are displaced by the machines.

Too bad we
could not turn this thing off.

These good things we do not fear; these good things this present government fear, for which they have no answer. There are some things we in this group fear, Mr. Speaker. We fear the centralization of power that somehow or other does gradually by stealth take charge of the people of Canada. In order to keep men free the principle of decentralization must be adopted. We have to get back to the place where there is decentralization of power, with more

I believe that is a principle which should be heeded throughout all our legislation, no matter what it is. For instance, the municipalities in this country are suffering.

speechtext: Order. I am extremely sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am obliged to advise him that his time has expired.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was not aware that time was slipping by so quickly. I shall pursue the matter at some future time. Thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that I am capable of doing it, but since the hon. member who has just folded his wings and sat down took us on a trip through the clouds, I should like to try to bring us back to earth.
Before I proceed with my main remarks I should like to join the other hon. members of my party in extending congratulations to my new leader. While it was a tragedy to lose a great Canadian, as Hon. George Drew, our former leader, was, nevertheless it was very interesting to learn that out of that tragedy and the events that followed one certain thing emerged, namely that the great Progressive Conservative party is a fighting and vital force in this country. It is on the march again; it is a national party. Regardless of what the last speaker said, Mr. Speaker, it is quite within the realm of possibility that it will form the next government of Canada under our new leader.
I also wish to join with my leader and other hon. members and express my sincere regrets at the loss of Hon. George Drew. Like other hon. members, I hope for his sake and that of Mrs. Drew that he shall have a full and complete restoration to health, because he is a great Canadian. Because of his experience, his knowledge and ability, with a complete restoration to health I am sure he will have a great contribution to make to the building of this nation and the country which he certainly loves.
Since I last spoke in this house and since the last general session we have lost two members of this party. I refer to the late Miss Sybil Bennett and Dr. Trainor. These two people contributed much not only to parliament but to the public service in general and also to their own communities, and we all regret their untimely passing. If I 

might be permitted to mention one other individual, I should like to pay my respects to a man who was born and lived all his life in my constituency. I refer to the late Senator Pirie, who passed on since parliament closed last year. He was a man who throughout his life gave a great many of his years to public service, first in our legislature where he *sat as an ordinary member and later on held the important portfolio of minister of lands and mines. He was one of the outstanding successful businessmen of the maritime provinces. If he was not the largest potato grower in the maritime provinces he was certainly one of them. He built up a great reputation for being a reliable shipper of seed stock potatoes; he was interested in manufacturing as well, and I know I speak for a large number of the citizens of my constituency when I say we certainly regret his passing at the early age at which he died.
Since it is the custom-but I should like to make it a little more sincere than that- I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hanna) on his address. It was very interesting to listen to him and to learn that he comes from a province and city which are among the richest and fastest growing in Canada. After listening to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) one would almost think that all this rapid growth and richness came to the province and the city of the mover of the address as a result of their happening to have a Social Credit government. That is something I shall have to look into a little further to see which one of them deserves the most credit.
However, I would like to extend congratulations particularly to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), one of our own provincial representatives, who seconded the address. I think his remarks were well delivered and they will be well received. He acquitted himself well. He mentioned one or two things, and I certainly have no quarrel with him about them. In that connection I might say I was rather well pleased that the Prime Minister realized that in his large family he had a supporter from New Brunswick, because it has been quite a long time since we have been remembered. It may be that the Prime Minister also realizes it is just possible this is the last opportunity he will have of doing honour to a member from New Brunswick, at least for a while.

I now come to the speech from the throne. It is not a long document. There is not very much in it with which I intend to deal. A great deal of it has to do with foreign affairs, national and international policy, with which I would be incapable of dealing anyway. But there are one or two things in it to which I feel I can give my full support. The first one I should like to mention is the increased grants to universities. We shall have a bill coming before us which we shall be able to study to understand the method by which those grants will be administered. When this government, or any other government, is prepared to improve the educational system of this country it can depend on me for what little support I can give it. Our institutions of learning, the people in charge of them, our teachers, professors, and so on, who have charge of the youth of our land, are possibly the most important institutions and people to whom we can give consideration. They have a great deal to do with the moulding of the youth of our nation. This contact takes place in the formative years, when young people commence to consider what their outlook in life should be and prepare to make the important choices which will confront them. They should be taught in the educational institutions by the finest minds in the country in order to lead them into wise consideration of what would be the best form of government and administration in order to maintain in the country a great free democracy such as we enjoy today. Any support for universities and those connected with them is a thing for which this or any other government should receive applause.
I notice that another bill will be brought before us concerning the renewing on a revised and enlarged basis the federal program of grants to provincial governments in aid of technical and vocational training. This is something about which I have been talking for two years, and I am extremely pleased to see that the government is going to bring before the house this session a bill to revise and increase these grants.
I happen to have in my constituency a vocational school. Although it is not large it is one of the older schools in this country and the staff is very proud of it; indeed, all of us are proud of the graduates of that school. There is also an agricultural department connected with it, and graduates from
The Address-Mr. Montgomery the school are filling important positions today all across Canada. I do not have a list of them and I could not begin to name them all, but a few months ago the director named for me a group of young men who have graduated from the agricultural department of that vocational school and are holding important and challenging posts all across Canada in work dealing with agriculture in one or another of its aspects.
I would like to confine the main body of my remarks to my own province and constituency. Agriculture is the chief industry not only in my own constituency but in the province of New Brunswick, and lumbering comes next. These two industries affect our economic life more than any others, and I would like first to say a word about lumbering.
I was recently speaking to a young man who had been in the lumbering business with his father and later carried on the business in partnership with his brothers. In order to keep the record straight let me point out that he is not of the same political faith as I am, but he came to me because I am a member of parliament. In discussing the lumbering business he said to me, "This tight money policy, the restriction of credit and the actions of the Bank of Canada are making it very difficult for lumbermen". He continued, "When you get to Ottawa look into this matter, and waste no time in trying to impress upon those people down there that this tight money policy may be all right for Ontario or some of the other provinces but it is actually hurting us in New Brunswick, and especially those who operate small businesses".
I am passing that along through you, Mr. Speaker, to the government to show that complaints are being made concerning the restriction of credit and the high interest rates that have been imposed by the Bank of Canada, and that these are actually harming some of our small industries.
As I have said, agriculture is our prime industry in the province of New Brunswick, but as was pointed out by the hon. member for Gloucester when he was speaking the other day, mining is rapidly emerging as an important aspect of the industrial development of our province. This has come about through the expansion of our power resources which we launched upon in the last few years, and this expansion must be continued.

The Address-Mr. Montgomery
When the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) spoke he implied that many people in the province are opposing such developments as the Passamaquoddy project. I want to assure him and other hon. members that those members from New Brunswick with whom I have spoken are just as much interested in this project as is the hon. member for Charlotte. V7e are sincerely hoping that the surveys will indicate that it is a feasible project. I found it interesting that he should tell us in plain terms that if it was found to be feasible the federal government would back us in the development.
That came as good news to me. I do not know how much authority the hon. member has, but I will say this. The federal authorities could back us on this and similar power developments without it costing them a cent. We could then finance some of our bigger projects and save our people a great deal of money. In addition we would be able to sell our power at a more attractive price and thereby attract more small industry to the province.
In spite of all the things I have mentioned I think the people of New Brunswick generally have had a very good year. The spirit which now exists in the province is different from the spirit which prevailed a few years ago, and although our economy is not forging ahead it is more than holding its own among the other provinces of Canada. At the risk of being accused of boasting I am going to suggest that much of this has been brought about because of the fact that we have been assisted and encouraged and given new leadership by an able provincial administration which works as much as it can in full co-operation with the federal authorities.
I might point out that the federal government will never lose anything by giving fuller co-operation to the present administration in New Brunswick. I challenge any hon. member from New Brunswick to stand up in this house and say that the money which goes to New Brunswick is being used for political purposes. Such statements could not be supported because they are without truth or foundation; I know what I am talking about.
Our province like some other parts of the maritimes did lag behind for a number of years. We did not have the revenue to meet the demands which piled up, and the requirements are enormous in the fields of education, hospitalization and health. The province


can do only so much by itself. We have a province containing many roads and bridges, many of which have deteriorated or are in bad shape. These must be restored, repaired and replaced by new ones, and all this construction will take a tremendous toll of the revenue available to the province.
I wish now to pass on to another matter referred to in the speech from the throne. I refer to the establishment of a committee to consider what should be done to make better use of land for agriculture and thus to contribute more effectively to the improvement of agricultural production and the incomes of those engaged in it. I have no quarrel with this and I offer no particular criticism of it, but in listening to the Prime Minister's speech on this matter the other day I could not help but feel that at best this is a longterm project. From that standpoint I have no criticism to make, but the farmers of the maritimes are looking for results which will come a little faster than that. They should have had assistance in 1956, and they are looking for assistance in 1957.
After listening to the Prime Minister and reading that statement in the speech from the throne it would appear to me that apparently this government have the feeling that our farmers are backward, are more or less ignorant and have very little knowledge of farming, where to farm or how to select land. That seems to me a mistaken idea. I want to say to hon. members of this house that some of the cleverest men are farmers. Some of the most successful men in our province are farmers.
I do not see any need to set up a committee which will cost this country hundreds of thousands of dollars in order to run around the country to find out if farmers know where to get land on which to farm, how to select land, or what crops to grow. All you have to do is assist the agriculturist by providing markets in which he can sell the products he raises at a reasonable profit. If that is done he will produce the goods. I challenge anyone to take issue with that statement. The farmers are able to pick out land, and they will move from place to place if it is profitable to do so. In other words they will be able to find out what are the best crops to grow on their land, and there is no need of a committee running around the country telling them to do that. What our farmers need are markets in which to sell their produce at a reasonable return.
There are other ways in which our farmers can be assisted. At the moment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is not in his seat but no doubt what I am about to say will be

The Address-Mr. Montgomery
called to his attention, because I believe his department is responsible for the administration of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. It will be recalled that when an amendment to this act was being considered last session it was pointed out that the farmers were not getting the type of assistance to which they felt they were entitled and which the framers of this legislation intended they should get.
I am sure almost every hon. member has had cases brought to his attention, and as a matter of fact the hon. member for Gloucester mentioned this legislation in his remarks the other day.
One case came to my attention which was so ridiculous that I cannot refrain from bringing it to the attention of the house and the Minister of Finance. A young man in his twenties, raised on a farm, married and with a family, owns one parcel of land consisting of 150 acres on which is a fairly good house which could not be built today for less than $5,000. In addition he owns another parcel of 100 acres on which is a much better house. Against that parcel of land there is an obligation of not more than $1,500, and there is nothing against the 150 acres. The two parcels of land are situated side by side. This man has a good deal of machinery, and as he lives quite close to his father they are able to exchange labour. He raised 5,000 barrels of potatoes this year, of which he still has 2,000 barrels in his potato house, a good portion of which he will have for sale.
He went to the Canadian farm loan for a loan of $3,000 because he wanted to build a stock barn which would cost him at least $6,000. He wanted to put up a modern barn on the 150 acres, but his request for a loan of $3,000 was turned down. I understand he was told that his buildings were not of sufficient value to warrant a loan under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. As I say, his request for a loan was turned down.
But that is not going to stop him. This young man was born and brought up in this particular community. He is a successful farmer, as his family have been before him. He is going to get help, but the burden will be greater because his payments will be more and the interest rate greater than if he could get a loan from the Canadian farm loan board. In my opinion he should have been able to get that loan if this legislation is on our statute books to assist good farmers.
The necessary lumber for this barn is already at the mill ready to be processed into boards. This young man is going to go ahead with that barn but, as I say, he should not have been turned down when he presented a proposition like that. I am
afraid that the department has set up this Canadian farm loan board as a type of bank where a man must be able to put up two or three dollars in order to borrow one dollar as a loan. Other applications have come to my attention which I admit were not so glaring; therefore I am saying nothing about them. But there is a happy medium, and that is why I bring this case to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I hope they will see that the administration of the Canadian Farm Loan Act is loosened up some. I know the people will appreciate that.
A farmer must sell his produce on fluctuating markets and he must depend upon the weather in order to carry on his harvesting and so on. All these things make farming hazardous. As you all know I am interested in the potato industry, as a great many of my people depend upon the growing of potatoes for their livelihood. Some of our young farmers are seeing what they can do to overcome the transportation problem and the fact that their markets are so far from home.
This brings me to another matter which I hope will be brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance. In raising potatoes the grower is faced with high freight rates and the fact that he has no protection. Then to add insult to injury as far as the growers of potatoes are concerned, they are faced with a 4 per cent premium on the Canadian dollar. Neighbours of ours within 14 miles, just across the border, are able to ship their potatoes into Montreal and other cities and towns in Quebec and Ontario and lay them down at a lower price than can our farmers.
The one item of 4 cents on the dollar amounts to considerable on a carload of potatoes. A car will hold 240 to 250 barrels, and that premium represents a profit of about 10 to 11 cents a barrel. That is what our farmers are up against. There are three young men in our community, men who were brought up on the farm, men who are potato growers and who have shown that they are good businessmen. They have launched a new frozen fruit and vegetable industry and propose to freeze French fried potatoes, and in so doing to handle several thousand barrels of potatoes. Those potatoes would be brought into the plant from within 20 or 25 miles, processed and then shipped in smaller bulk to the markets of Canada. By this means an opportunity will be given to the small farmer who can grow a few potatoes or strawberries or small vegetables and whose produce can be sent to the factory by truck or car.
I notice that neither the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) nor the Minister of

Labour Conditions-C.P.R. Strike Labour (Mr. Gregg) is present in the house, but perhaps some other member would convey this to them, because it is, maybe, the first time I have wished to pass them a bouquet. I want to thank the Minister of Labour and the right hon. Minister of Agriculture for the consideration they showed toward these young men in co-operation with the province of New Brunswick in the erection of this plant. When he was approached the Minister of Agriculture told me last spring they would do what they could to help, and I wish now to say that we are pleased with what they did.
Since this plant was put in operation it has been found that the cottonseed oil which is imported in order to process these farm products has to carry a tariff of 20 per cent or more, which means a considerable burden on the cost of processing. In the letter I have it is stated that from 20 to 30 per cent of the cost is due to this oil. The operators find that the reason a tariff has been placed on it is because the same oil is imported for the manufacture of margarine. I am not surprised. I am glad there is a tariff on the importation of a substance for use in the manufacture of margarine because margarine, when manufactured, goes on the market in competition with an agricultural product. Therefore, I say, we should protect our agricultural product and put on a tariff when necessary. However, there is a point which I would like to ask the Minister of Finance to take into consideration.

I have here a proposal to terminate the interruption of transportation services on the Canadian Pacific Railway lines which has just been signed by Mr. Crump for the company and Mr. Gamble for the union.
A commission consisting of three judges to be constituted under the Inquiries Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 154, 

and to have the benefit of any technical advice it requires from the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and from any other public body it deems advisable. This act provides that the commission may engage the services of technical advisers or other experts to aid and assist the commission in its inquiry.
In view of the establishment of this commission, an agreement shall be entered into by the parties, including the present diesel rule, arbitraries and mountain differential, which diesel rule, arbitraries and mountain differential shall be subject to amendment by renegotiation in the light of the advisory report of the commission.
The terms and conditions of the agreement in respect of all outstanding matters other than the diesel rule, arbitraries and mountain differential shall be in accordance with the report of the conciliation board.
Transportation services will be resumed forthwith.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY

It is suggested that the commission begin its inquiry as soon as possible and that it report not later than October 1, 1957. The understanding is that immediate notices are going out to all concerned, and that work to get the transportation services into operation will start not later than daylight tomorrow morning.
I think hon. members will wish me to express on their behalf and on behalf of all the Canadian people appreciation for the serious and genuine efforts which have been made by those representing both parties to this dispute to eliminate the differences which occasioned the interruption of transportation services; and that the parties will realize that in bringing about a speedy resumption of transportation services they will be rendering not only to those people they represent but to the whole Canadian people a very much appreciated service and one for which all will, I think, be grateful. I think the gratitude and good will which will radiate from this short document will help to restore good will between the company and its employees, a good will that means so much to the successful service of the public by the transportation system.

We
certainly welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister. The very fact that three judges have been allotted to this important inquiry and that they can obtain all the technical assistance they require should be the means of bringing down a report which I hope will settle this problem. We are happy to know, too, that the problem of the diesels will be separated from the other problems that will be dealt with by the parties concerned. We, too, express satisfaction that there has been no compulsion; free men in a free society, bargaining freely, have achieved the result, and that is very much to the good. I am glad there was no compulsion exercised against either party in this dispute, and I am sure the people of Canada will welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister. I wish to congratulate all those who have participated in bringing about this satisfactory result.

Mr. Speaker, I had been making a few remarks concerning the importation of cottonseed oil, which is a matter of interest to a young industry in my constituency. My chief argument is that while there could be a tariff against the oil when it is brought in and processed with other materials to make a manufactured product which is on the market in competition with agricultural products, I think when the oil is brought in to process an agricultural product itself in order to put that product on the market there could be some way in which the oil could be reclassified, in the same way that soy bean oil brought in for the processing or canning of fish is allowed to come in free. I leave that with the hope that the Minister of Finance and his officials will give every consideration to the matter.
There is another matter I should like to mention, and my plea in this instance is also made to the Minister of Finance. I want to assure him briefly that the greatest complaint of the potato producers of New Brunswick is that regardless of what the tariff board found they do want a tariff or some arrangement made whereby Canadian potatoes may enter the United States market on the same terms as potatoes from that country enter the Canadian market. The Address-Mr. Montgomery
I am not going to say much about freight rates at this time except to say, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) said, that it is time a new look was taken at the Maritime Freight Rates Act. In the light of the increases in freight rates that have taken place, the act should be revamped so we will get the benefits that it was originally intended that the east would get.
I should also like to say a word or two about veterans affairs. I am not going to spend very much time on the matter, not because it is not an important subject but because there are other veterans in the house who as a rule can present the subject much better than I can. But I support the brief the Canadian Legion submitted to the government wherein they ask in particular that the ceilings on total permissible incomes under the War Veterans Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 and $2,000. I also feel very strongly that Canadian veterans of world war I whose overseas service was restricted to the United Kingdom should be eligible for the war veterans allowance, provided that their service in the United Kingdom was of at least one year's duration.
There is another submission by the Legion that I certainly think deserves serious consideration, namely that the widows of allied ex-servicemen be granted the war veterans allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada, provided that the effective date of her eligibility be 20 years after the husband's arrival to take up permanent residence in Canada, that the widow herself has completed 20 years' residence in Canada, and that both the husband and wife under all other circumstances would be entitled to the pension.
There is one other thing that seems to me to be rather unfair, and it is something I did not know existed. Section 8 of the War Veterans Allowance Act reads:
No allowance shall be paid in respect of any orphan who is in receipt of a pension under the Pension Act.
This section has the effect of refusing to children of men who died in action, or as the result of service disabilities, the same level of income as that provided to orphans under the War Veterans Allowance Act. An orphan under the War Veterans Allowance Act can be financially assisted up to a maximum of $720 per year, but because of this restrictive section, that is section 8 of the War Veterans Allowance Act, an orphan under the Canadian Pension Act, even where there is no other income, is limited to $480 per year. This appears to be a very unjust situation.
I strongly support the Legion in these demands. There are some others which may


not be so necessary, such as the one respecting the permissive equity value in a home, although it must be said that values have gone up greatly since the provision was originally enacted. They also ask in their brief for an increase in general disability pensions. I am not going to say anything about that, but I do say that I support particularly the requests to which I have referred, and I support generally the brief of the Canadian Legion.
As I said a minute ago, I do not have much to say about the strike. I did not intend to say very much because others have spoken fully. My area is going to be very pleased at the settlement, because it was very badly tied up. However, I do want to refer to one assertion made by the hon. member for Charlotte that we from the maritimes do not come to the federal authorities with any sound ideas. I do not agree with him. I do not think it is a fair statement to make.
I want to tell the house, Mr. Speaker, that in the Atlantic provinces economic council, ordinarily referred to as APEC, I think we have a group of sincere men working together and when their ideas are submitted they should not be called cockeyed, as the hon. member did in referring to them this morning. I think it is unfair. I have a lot of faith in APEC. I am satisfied they are doing a good job and are going to do a better job for the maritime provinces. I am satisfied, regardless of what was said this morning, that the federal government will pay some attention and give a good hearing to the ideas brought forth by the Atlantic provinces economic council.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to devote any time to congratulating the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It has been done so often that I think it can be taken for granted that we all echo the sentiments of our leaders who tendered congratulations in the first instance.
I am going to try to be specific in what I say. I listened with a great deal of attention this afternoon to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). While we may not agree with all he had to say, I think we can agree that he livened the house up and put the situation in its proper perspective. This is an election session. Many of us will not be here next session, and it is well that we pay our respects to each other before we leave. But I think it is particularly necessary that, before leaving here, we make ourselves clear as to why we may want to come back. The hon. member for Macleod rather paved the way. Of

The Address-Mr. Gillis
course, as far as he is concerned, no one is coming back next session except Social Credit members.
This year the throne speech is a rather puzzling one. The fact of the matter is that, when I read it over, my opinion was that this being an election year, the government are being extremely careful in anything they may propose by way of legislation. They are not sure what is best to do so far as the country is concerned. Hence they figured that if they brought in a speech from the throne with nothing in it that was controversial, the members of the house when discussing it for the next 10 days would give the government an idea as to what they should do this session by way of legislation to supplement the speech from the throne. In other words, in my judgment it is just a trial balloon. There is not anything to disagree with; there is not anything to agree with, very much. We shall just be obliged to tell the government what we think is best for the Minister of Finance to do in his budget and what they should bring in by way of legislation at this session, as we see it, if they want to get elected again in the country.
I think the puzzler for the government at this time is the question whether the Minister of Finance should use his present surplus for the purpose of reducing taxes or whether he should use it for the purpose of building up social security payments right along the line. Before I get through I am going to tell him in no uncertain terms what I think he should do. I believe that is what the government want us to do.
For a start, let me say this. The throne speech does one thing that is necessary, though I do not think it goes far enough and I do not think it is equal as between province and province. I refer to federal aid to education. There is a great disparity between the disbursements in the maritime provinces and in the rest of Canada. I have here a clipping reporting the speech of a learned professor who was making an analysis of the subject. It is quite lengthy. He goes into the matter rather fully. However, he makes this observation dealing with the proposal to double the amount of money available for university aid:
Assuming the announced doubling of last year's amount of federal grant to universities a university in Alberta will receive $300 per student and one in Ontario, $275. A university in Nova Scotia, however, will receive $160 for rendering the same service to the nation, Dr. Kerr said.
While we all believe that making available that additional money is a step in the right direction, I believe the equalization of those
payments as between province and province is something that should be taken under consideration. There is no reason why the amount per student should vary so greatly as between universities in the maritimes and the other universities across the country. Of course another provision forecast in the throne speech is to boost the aid to technical high schools and trade centres. The money had run out. New agreements are now available which provide for much more money. It is a development that is badly needed across the country. That is another thing for which this throne speech has provided. Of course the details will have to be worked out as between the provinces and the federal government.
There is another good thing that was in the throne speech-I picked out all that was good in it, and there were only three things- was the increased aid for disabled seamen. The federal compensation act is being revised and brought into line with the compensation acts in the provinces, and the pension to the widow of a seaman who may have lost his life is now being equalized as it is paid from province to province. These are the three things that were of value in the throne speech. In view of the fact that I consider it to be a trial balloon and that the government are looking for advice as to what they might bring down, I am going to try to tell them from there on in.

That is exactly right, and it is an extremely easy matter to iron out. It is merely a matter of a little bit of arithmetic.
I should like to say just one or two words about the announcement made by the Prime Minister a few moments ago. I am not going to hold any post mortem on the matter, but I should just like to say this. This country today is going through a process of industrialization that is a new industrial revolution. I view that strike on the C.P.R. as one of the reflex pains of automation. It happens not only on the C.P.R.; it is happening in every industry in the country. Technological advance-and we must accept it-brings about these things. We had it in the mining industry. We had it in the automobile industry. Now we have it on the railways.
158	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gillis
I think the government will be obliged to provide certain machinery, and I think it is simple to provide it. We have been advocating it for years. I believe the government should set up industrial councils by means of which representatives from every industry in the country would be able to meet with the government, with representatives of management, and the unions called in whenever there was a threatened disturbance because of technological advance. The matter is not going to stop there. That machinery is today necessary so the Department of Labour at least would have a ready contact with people in the industry who know the repercussions of any changes that may be taking place.
The building industry has had that machinery for years. You never hear of any trouble in the building industry. They have had their own industrial council for many years and they come in here and meet with the minister and his officials, both management and employees, and iron out their difficulties before they get started. That is prevention. In these matters, as with disease, prevention is better than a cure. It is better to prevent an appendix eruption than to have an operation. If you had had an industrial council of the railway industry, with competent people who had seen that strike developing, and if they had met together before the eruption, I am reasonably sure that it would not have taken place.
I just say that now in passing because I think the government should take advantage of that kind of machinery. It does not cost them anything. It is merely a matter of having the personnel appointed from each industry and from the railroads so that when something like what has happened occurs they have someone to whom to go rather than being left to get out in the street and fight it out among themselves, and disrupt either that industry or the economy of the country, as happened in this case. I hope the Minister of Labour particularly and the government will give some thought to that, because we have been preaching it for 10 years. The example of the building trades is a good one, because any friction is ironed out before there are any difficulties.
I said a moment ago that if we are leaving here to go back for an election we should be quite clear in our own minds where we stand and for what we stand. This morning-and I am not saying this to be mean-I listened to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) speak. I always enjoy his speeches. He took the Gordon report-
