speechtext:
They are not going to take this bit by bit, taking the good and leaving out the bad. I just want to warn my hon. friend, because that will be held against him at the right time and in the right place, not by me but by people sitting not very far from him. If I were living close to the hon. member I would make full use of it, too, and I know he would if the positions were reversed.
I know this is an interim report of the Gordon commission and the final report may be much different. I hope it is. There is not anything new in it. I am going to deal particularly with the maritime sections of it. He pretty well writes off the maritimes. I am dealing particularly with the coal industry now, because he made a special study of the coal industry. On page 51 of the report there is a table headed, "The Estimated Sources or Types of Energy Used in Canada". This table shows how the coal industry has declined and will decline by 1980. It shows coal, including coal for electrical energy, as a percentage of the total energy consumed. In 1926 it was 69 per cent; in 1953, 39 per cent; and by 1980 it will only be 16 per cent. That is not a very bright picture.
Then, again, over on page 103 of the report, in the first paragraph on the page he dealt with the mechanization taking place in the mines. He said:
This means, according to estimates contained in our study on the Nova Scotia coal industry, that if there were no reduction in employment an additional two million tons of coal would be produced each year. On the other hand, if production is not increased the services of some 4,000 of the 11,000 mine workers presently employed will not be required.
Knowing the industry as I do, he is practically telling me there will be 4,000 more

people go out of that industry. There has been a heavy exodus from it in the last five years.
Over in another section of this report on the maritimes he tells us that he sees the future of Nova Scotia coal marketing as being backed up into the maritime provinces only. Of course he advocates the development of thermal power to supplement the power at Gagetown through the use of coal from Nova Scotia. Well, that is not a new story; that is the Christie report. We have heard all that over the years. So far as I am concerned there is nothing in the report with respect to the maritime provinces except a reiteration of the policies that have been in effect for the last 50 years. He says to move out. We have been moving out for the last 50 years, and there is nothing in the report that would suggest that there is any future development for the maritime provinces.
He makes one recommendation here with which I agree, although the mechanics are not exactly as I would like to see them. Over the years I have advocated a national energy policy. In this report he recommends a national energy board which would replace the present coal board. It is not necessary to replace that coal board. All you need to do is amend the act under which that board is set up, broaden the powers of the board and give it the necessary technical personnel to examine coal, gas, electricity and any other fuel that may develop in the future. He says the board should supervise imports, exports and so forth, but I would add "regulation", because if you have no power to regulate you have no power to direct. If it were merely a matter of advising as between the provinces and federal government and the industry, then it would not be a very effective board. At least he has taken a step in the direction that I have been advocating for some considerable time.
I hope before a final report is written the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will have some consultations with Mr. Gordon in order to enable Mr. Gordon to understand the problem as it really is. You have to have a board with the proper personnel, but you do not have to replace the coal board. If you broadened the board and added to it, then you could give it the power of regulation to make it effective.
According to press reports, coal is far from dead. It is one of the main problems of the Russians today. I have a newspaper report written by Victor Riesel, the correspondent who writes for the New York Mirror and who was blinded not so long ago by gangsters of the labour movement in the United States. I am not going to read the
The Address-Mr. Gillis full report, but according to it the great difficulty Russia is having today, and one of the main reasons for the uprisings in the satellite countries, is that the miners are not producing coal. He says it was the miners in Hungary who spearheaded that revolution. The interesting part of the story to me is that there is a tremendous market in West Germany and in France for coal from this continent. He says:
You get a picture of just what the Hungarian mines mean to Moscow if you look at the needs of the Germans and French. The western Germans, for example, would be happy if they could increase their purchase of 8 million tons of coal annually to 15 million. They've flown over some of their top industrialists to see John L. and coal industry leaders here. They'll get the tonnage if we can put ships to sea.
The French have had their people here too, seeking an increase from 3 million tons to 7 million tons a year. Compare these figures-which the French and Germans reckon can keep their industries alive-with what the Russians are losing just in Hungary.
It is a good story and points out the fact that coal is far from dead. In this Gordon report there is the observation that there is a tremendous market for coal in Europe, provided we can get the proper subsidy understanding with the federal government. I am saying this just as a warning; we do not want to close out our coal industry in this country too fast. I am reasonably sure also that if a competent examination is made by this Gordon commission of the economics of laying a pipe line to bring natural gas from Alberta to Quebec and Montreal and changing your equipment over to use that gas, and compare that with the economics of coal in that area, coal will stay in that area. I am reasonably sure that would happen. I hope that before the final report is written something will be done on that particular matter.
I hear everybody talking about an increase in population. That increase is taking place in almost every section of Canada except the maritimes. I was looking at some figures on urban centres issued in 1956. I note that in the province of Nova Scotia, instead of there being an increase from 1951 to 1956, there has been a decrease of 11,000. I know in my own particular area, in two or three towns, we have lost around 1,840 people, and the trend is in that direction.
In his report Mr. Gordon has said very little about the rehabilitation of agriculture in the maritimes. One of the main reasons why agriculture is not developing in that province in the way it should is the cost of fertilizer. We are dragging fertilizer all the way down from Ontario. The government, of course, is subsidizing the freight rate on it, but even after it gets there it is very expensive. A few

The Address-Mr. Gillis days ago I was interested in picking up another report which shows that there is a complete lack of thinking in our part of the country with respect to the use of our own resources. This article has a startling headline, as follows: "Charges Fertilizer Source Neglected". The article says:
Some 100,000 tons of material that should be going on Nova Scotia farm soil is being wasted every year at the steel industry in Sydney, Dr. G. R. Smith, chairman of the soils and fertilizer committee at the Truro agricultural college, told the Nova Scotia agricultural conference here yesterday.
This is quite a lengthy article. The 100,000 tons referred to consist of slag, waste from the steel plant. I remember an estimate going through this house in 1942 that gave the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation a substantial sum of money for research into the possibilities of using that slag for fertilizer or whether it should be treated, and so forth. Evidently its possibilities were proven, and according to this article by this man, who is an expert, it is an excellent fertilizer, as good as any they are hauling from Ontario. Well, that is the kind of thing Mr. Gordon should look into.
I believe that the agricultural industry in that part of the country should be stepped up. I do not think any country can survive long whose main basis is not agriculture, because people have to eat. You can make as many automobiles and steel plants as you like; you can produce as much manufactured goods as you like, but you still have to come back to the farmers of the country in order to feed the people.
This report also indicates that on a national scale our farm population is going to decline terrifically by 1980. This is something the federal government should definitely take a look at, because we just cannot afford to keep on crowding people into urban centres, building skyscrapers, putting children into those buildings and cooping them up like chickens where they have no fresh air and no place to play or to do anything else. I believe a country that neglects its agriculture and does not maintain it as its main base will pay for it before very long. That was the forecast of the economists who assisted in compiling the report.
If we have 100,000 tons of good fertilizer which has been thrown away in that part of the country, then I ask this question. Why could it not be utilized and given to the farmers? It could be given to them at very low cost, and it might encourage them if they do not have to pay $90 or $100 a ton for fertilizer, as they are doing today. I mention that because I think it is something the federal government should take a look at.

The federal government has already put money into the project in the research stage, and according to the report I read it has proved practicable. It was good fertilizer but it has been thrown away.
Of course one could go on and on with the Gordon report, but I am not going to do that. There are many things I would like to say about it, but I should like to save them until I see the final report. This is only a sketchy thing, but it definitely pinpoints the mari-times. They made a special examination of the coal industry and other resources, but they certainly did not come up with anything. The recommendations in the report with respect to the kind of public investment fund for the purpose of assisting industry are quite all right. It is quite all right to set up a fund of that kind. That has already been done in the maritimes. There is a provincial public investment fund today, but in addition to that we have the Atlantic provinces economic council which is doing the research, and then we have industrial development boards in many sections of the province.
Some of these boards are bringing small industry into certain sections. I know that right in my own area a plant was recently established with local capital by the local industrial development board. This plant will employ some 300 people. This is the kind of development I like to see. If a plant locates in the province, the investment fund in the province will grant a dollar for every dollar invested by the plant itself. They will be assisted by the provincial government advancing dollar for dollar.
The economic council shows me, at least, that there is no need to appoint a new body to come in to do that kind of work. They are doing it themselves. The men who are doing that work are men who are living in the province and know the needs of the province and the marketing possibilities of the province, and have an idea as to how much interprovincial marketing can be done, because this is one of the main objectives of the organization. As I said before, they have their own industrial boards in different sections which are raising funds locally and are trying to bring in small industries.
If the federal government goes along with the Gordon recommendation that a fund should be set up by the federal government to assist in the rehabilitation of those areas, it should be done in co-operation with the province to supplement work already being done by those boards. Full advantage should be taken of the Atlantic provinces economic council and the facilities they can supply locally in all four provinces. It would be the best machinery that could be set up.

I am glad to see the Minister of Finance entering the chamber. Before he came in I was telling the house that the throne speech, with very few exceptions, was a trial balloon. I did not see much in it. It leaves a lot for the members to say. The suggestion is, let the members talk on this speech and by the time the minister is ready to write his budget he will have a fairly good idea as to whether he should reduce taxes because of his surplus, or whether he should step up social security payments all along the line. Of course other legislation can be brought in despite the fact that there is not much in the speech from the throne.
Well, I would like to tell the minister that as far as I am concerned there are many people in this country who would get no relief from a tax cut. The last time the minister of finance, now Mr. Justice Abbott, presented his budget speech, he pointed out that there were 137,000 families in the country living on incomes below the income tax level, and they received no relief from a tax cut. If the minister was considering using that surplus I would suggest the way he could get the greatest political value from it across the country would be, as a start, to step up the old age pension to the figure of $60 a month, I would say, because that is needed. These people are living on the borderline of charity, and those who do not have relatives or friends who will assist them are in a worse position than borderline charity cases.
It would be a good gesture on the part of the minister if he would step up the old age security pension, and I believe the second thing he could do would be to remove the means test from the blind pension. These people are already penalized as it is; they are living in darkness. Those who are able to go out and supplement that pension by some income should not be further penalized and the income should not militate against their right to retain the $40 a month, as it does today. It would be a good idea to bring the blind pension up to a par with the old age security pension.
A third step would be to modify the regulations of the Old Age Assistance Act. I believe the qualification age of 65 is too high. In large part these people are disabled through sickness or by some other means and have no income. I believe the qualification age should be lowered to 60 in the case of men and 50 in the case of women. The most pathetic figure in our midst is the woman of 50 years of age who has raised a family, now broken in health, whose children are away, who is without a home and who lives with friends and neighbours. Any hon. member who has done any work in his riding must 82715-11
The Address-Mr. Gillis know of many cases like that which come to his attention, and there is nothing one can tell these women. It is a very sad thing to have to tell a woman in those circumstances that there is nothing one can do because there is no legislation.
A fourth step would be a modification of the Disabled Persons Act, and we have been hammering at this now for a couple of years. Today you can live in a wheel chair, but if you are able to wheel yourself to the table and eat you cannot qualify for a pension under this act. You may even be mentally and physically incapacitated from birth and now 50 years of age. I know of some cases like that. Some of the people I know in this situation have never earned a dollar in their lives but they are able to walk, and therefore cannot qualify under the act. I am convinced there should be some modification in the administration of the act.
Of course all the things I have mentioned cost money, and the minister may not have enough money in the surplus to meet these needs. Nevertheless, another piece of social security that is a must is a national health plan. At some time in some way during this session an effort should be made to enable people across this country to secure medical attention at a nominal cost. The standards of medicine are high in this country, and we have many centres across Canada which are just as good as the Mayo clinic or other institutions in the United States. Personally if I required an operation of any kind I would not leave Halifax to have it performed, but thousands and thousands of Canadian people are unable to reach medical centres.
In my own community we maintain local medical institutions and on a panel basis we pay doctors in our hospitals, and this is true of many centres across Canada. It sometimes happens in small communities that one cannot get the attention which one requires, and some people must pay $1,000 to receive some attention in Halifax or elsewhere. Local hospitals today are going further and further into debt and their equipment is becoming more and more out of date. These hospitals expect that something will be done on a national basis, and they are not going out on drives to build up their resources because they believe a national health program will come into being, and I think it is essential at this time.
I believe the greatest relief the people of Canada could receive at this time would come if the government took the bit in its teeth and established a national health plan. I do not think it could be done under the formula laid down at the last dominion-provincial conference, which stipulated that

The Address-Mr. H. J. Murphy six provinces must consent and Ontario and Quebec must join. It will not be done on such a basis. With the exception of the western provinces the other provinces have not indicated their willingness to come in, and I think another formula must be devised. Realizing the need for this type of legislation, the federal government should take it upon itself to work out a formula that would perhaps make it easier for the provinces to accept such a plan, and something should be done at this session of parliament.
If the minister will accept my advice he will bring about the social security measures I have mentioned rather than reduce taxes, which gives very little relief except to those who are in the brackets where greater taxation must be paid. Those who are earning $5,000 and more per year do not require relief to the extent that it is required by those in the lower brackets. After all, it is not the amount of tax you pay but what you have left that counts.
If the minister could find his way clear to using some of that surplus in the various ways I have described, in stepping up the social security measures and bringing about a national health program, then he would be doing something for which I personally, and I am convinced people right across this country, would commend him.
I believe my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I will close by saying I trust that when the minister brings in his budget 1 will be able to stand up and vote for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member just one question. My recollection is that the party he belongs to has on other occasions advocated that we should increase the basic exemptions for married and single people to an extent which would more than dispose of my surplus. At this time I would like to ask him which he wants.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I thought I was quite clear, Mr. Speaker, when I said that as far as I am concerned if the minister will use his surplus for the purposes I enumerated in my address I would be quite satisfied to leave the tax structure as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All right.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to take part in this debate, and like many hon. members who have spoken previously I wish to congratulate the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), who is my seat mate, and the seconder, the hon. member for Gloucester

(Mr. Robichaud) who is a colleague of mine from my home province, New Brunswick.
I am pleased to hear the news that the C.P.R. strike has ended and the men are returning to work. Coming as I do from a railway city, in this case a Canadian National Railways city, where we have about 5,000 railway employees working in and out of the locality, you will understand my concern and interest in this matter. I know the employees of the C.N.R. in Moncton will be pleased to hear that their fellow workmen are returning to their jobs.
Unlike the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery), who expressed his sympathy over the loss of a senator from his county, I wish to express my happiness on the appointment of a new senator from the county of Westmorland. We now have a colleague in Ottawa, although he is in the other place, who is an expert on agriculture. Mr. Taylor served as minister of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick for a period of approximately 17 years. I will feel more confident now when matters relating to agriculture come up. We have listened to many people from other parts of the country bringing up agricultural problems pertaining to the west, of which they had expert knowledge, and I feel now that we have someone from the east who will be of assistance to us.
Nearly every time I have spoken in the House of Commons I have talked about the Chignecto canal. It did not seem to arouse very much interest, but I am not going to let the opportunity offered today go by without mentioning it. I hope that with the continual repetitious reference to this matter the canal will some day come into being.
As hon. members know, the proposed Chignecto canal would be 18 miles long, connecting Northumberland strait with the bay of Fundy and crossing the isthmus which now connects New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. This canal has been a subject of discussion in this house for many years and was actively under discussion long before I came to the chamber. With the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway ships will still have to go around the province of Nova Scotia when headed for the United States, Mexico or South America.
I believe that some day the government of the United States, as well as the government of this country, will consider the building of this canal to be a security measure, as it would afford a sheltered route from ports on the east coast of the United States such as New York and Boston to United States ports on the great lakes. Ships would be able to go from New York, Portland and Boston

to Chicago and other lake ports and take on and discharge cargo both coming and going. I feel that some day this matter probably will be better presented and more publicity given to it nationally.
All hon. members from New Brunswick at some time or other have indicated in the house their support of this project. I believe the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) expressed it at a public meeting held in Saint John, but I have heard the rest of the hon. members express their support of this proposal in this house. This project was implied at the time of confederation, and was considered to be a confederation promise. I hope the promise will be honoured some day. If the hon. members from the maritime provinces would be as consistently insistent as western hon. members are in presenting their problems, I feel that this matter would receive the publicity and attention it deserves. I am not going to go into the matter at great length, but I do hope someone else will bring it up and tell the house more about it, and perhaps be more persuasive in putting the matter before the house.
I should like now to bring up a few matters concerning my constituency. Recently the Department of Fisheries announced that between $150,000 and $200,000 would be spent over a three-year period to restock and rehabilitate the oyster fishing beds of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It is my earnest hope that some of this work will take place in the Northumberland strait, or parts of the Northumberland strait adjoining Westmorland county, and in that part of Kent county which adjoins Westmorland county. I appreciate that as far as coastal waters are concerned there is no real boundary between counties. A few years ago this area produced many good oysters, and I would be pleased if the Minister of Fisheries could give details of the work to be done in the rehabilitation and seeding of the oyster beds, as this would be of benefit to the different districts in the province of New Brunswick.
In connection with the fishing industry I should like to refer briefly to the conveniences and facilities for fishermen in the way of
The Address-Mr. H. J. Murphy wharves and dredging which have been provided, and to express my appreciation to the Minister of Public Works and the department for the new wharf recently completed at Emily's point at Shemogue. This project has been needed for some time and was built during the summer and fall of last year. It will fill a great need of the fishermen in that area.
Last year I referred to the need of extensions to certain existing wharves. Representations have been made to me on many occasions by fishermen along the coast of Westmorland county from Barachois to Cape Tormentine, setting out the need for wharf extensions in that area in order that they may be better able to land their fish. During the summer a great amount of dredging was done in many small harbours, and this enables fishermen to bring their boats in to unload at the wharves.
However, there are a few wharves which still require to be extended because of the increased fishing industry, and I would ask the Minister of Public Works to consider carefully the representations made by fishermen for increased wharf facilities at cape Bald, Dupuis Corner, Robichaud and Kouchi-bouguac river. These extensions are necessary because of the increased volume of business.
While I am speaking of wharves, I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the need for improvements to the wharf at Point du Chene. Years ago this was the terminal for the ferry operating between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, before the Cape Tormentine-Borden ferry was started. Besides being used by fishing boats, this wharf is used by sea-going vessels engaged in the pulpwood export trade.
On motion of Mr. Murphy (Westmorland) the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall continue with this debate on Monday and Tuesday.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
